#5 is discussing the general serialization format, but also mixes in the dev ux related discussion points.

My take-away from the discussions at IETF 126 was that people were pointing towards CDDL and defining CBOR and JSON in one CDDL. Make sure it is clear that we use CBOR over the wire, but have a clear definition of JSON representations for configuration, debugging, etc.
Copied over from the other issue:

If we use integer based maps in CBOR, we could in theory define in CDDL values that are different between CBOR and JSON representation which would allow us to define keys in the map that are different from CBOR (integer) and JSON (string). Taken from [cbor-wg Wiki](https://github.com/cbor-wg/cddl/wiki/Useful-CDDL#named-numbers):

```cddl
JC<"v", 2>
binary-value = JC<base64-string, bstr>
```
JC<"v",2> defines the value as `"v"` for JSON and `2` for  CBOR.

[RFC9741](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc9741) introduces control operators that allows to express things like base64 encoding in CDDL:

```cddl
signature-for-json = text .b64u signature
signature = bytes .cbor COSE_Sign1
```

items.body:
Section 5 requires: "For signed requests, the Verifier MUST use, and the Wallet MUST
accept the Client Identifier Prefix x509_hash". "MUST use" does not merely set an
interoperability floor; it forbids a Verifier from using any other mechanism even
inside an ecosystem whose wallets support one. The request here is surgical: in HAIP
1.1, change "MUST use" to "MUST support", keeping x509_hash as the mandatory baseline
every wallet and verifier implements, while permitting ecosystems to additionally use
`verifier_attestation` or `openid_federation` where bilaterally supported.

This is deliberately narrower than #88, which proposed adding or mandating OpenID
Federation at the organizational level and was closed for lack of consensus to
mandate, with wallet complexity as the recorded concern. This proposal adds zero
mandatory-to-implement surface for Wallets. It was also noted there that the WG's
direction meant dropping verifier attestation; we understand that as dropping it as a
mandate candidate while its attester trust was undefined. That gap is now being
addressed concretely: we have proposed in openid/federation-wallet#60 that the
attestation issuer be resolved through a Trust Chain, with the instance bound to the
organizational Credential Verifier that carries registered entitlements.

Two developments since #88 motivate revisiting, as its closing comment anticipated:

1. **Verifier instances.** Presentations are increasingly made to mass-deployed
   verifier software (POS terminals, mobile readers, proximity readers) with
   per-device keys and no resolvable identity. Under "MUST use x509_hash" their
   trust reduces to CA roots baked into wallet builds. The EUDI ARF's per-instance
   access certificates confirm the requirement while duplicating PKI outside any
   dynamic trust fabric; #371 documents the same pressure from New Zealand, where
   verifiers sit outside the trust framework entirely.

2. **x509_hash already depends on external trust infrastructure.** As raised in #243
   (unanswered), x509_hash provides no binding between the client identifier and
   redirect_uri/response_uri; that binding "must be established externally (e.g. by
   trust registries)". The mandated mechanism therefore already presupposes exactly
   the out-of-band trust registry function this proposal would let ecosystems
   operate in a standardized, resolvable form.

If the WG prefers HAIP itself to remain x509-only even at the "MUST support" level,
we will take up the alternative already suggested in #88 (a federation profile
layered on HAIP) and contribute it, including conformance test text. But correcting
the base profile avoids each ecosystem shipping "HAIP but with one thing changed",
the outcome #371's discussion argued against.
items.title: HAIP 1.1: change x509_hash from "MUST use" to "MUST support" so attested verifier instances are not foreclosed

items.body:
The specification models three entity types (Table 1): `openid_wallet_provider`,
`openid_credential_issuer`, `openid_credential_verifier`. The Wallet Provider exists
for an architectural reason: federation trust is established by resolution, and a
wallet instance is unresolvable. It is manufactured or installed software with no
queryable identity: it cannot serve an Entity Configuration at an https Entity
Identifier, cannot be listed or fetched by a superior, and its keys are generated per
installation. Attestation therefore substitutes for resolution: the provider is the
resolvable entity in the Trust Chain, and it attests the unresolvable instances.

Verifier instances are now in exactly the same position. A presentation is
increasingly made to a POS terminal, a mobile reader app, a proximity reader:
software with per-device keys and no resolvable identity of its own. Yet the
specification models the Credential Verifier only as an organizational leaf entity
and gives its instances no provider to attest them.

Central signing does not remove the need. Routing every request through the
organization's backend for signature fails offline and proximity flows (ISO/IEC
18013-5 reader authentication is per reader by construction), forces presentation
responses (encrypted to a key in the request) through the backend, and concentrates
one organizational key in every terminal so that a single compromise revokes the
organization. The EUDI ARF reaches the same conclusion: access certificates are
issued per Relying Party Instance. Its mechanism, however, is a parallel static x509
hierarchy (Access Certificate Authorities) outside any dynamic trust fabric, and
every other available mechanism shares that property:

- OpenID4VP `x509_san_dns` / `x509_hash`: CA roots baked into wallet software.
- OpenID4VP `verifier_attestation`: the artifact is fully defined
  (`typ: verifier-attestation+jwt`, key binding via `cnf`, `client_id` = `sub`), but
  the wallet's trust in the attester is explicitly undefined ("The `iss` claim value
  ... MUST identify a party the Wallet trusts"), so in practice attester keys are
  baked in.
- ISO/IEC 18013-5 reader authentication: reader CA lists distributed out of band.

## Proposed mechanism

Give verifier instances the pattern wallet instances already have, keeping two trust
statements separate:

1. **Entity type.** Define `openid_verifier_provider` (or generalize the Wallet
   Provider): an organizational entity, resolvable through the Trust Chain, that
   attests verifier instances.

2. **Instance attestation.** The provider issues short-lived Verifier Attestation
   JWTs exactly as defined by OpenID4VP: `sub` is the organizational Credential
   Verifier's Entity Identifier, `cnf` binds the per-instance key. This mirrors
   draft-ietf-oauth-attestation-based-client-auth (`sub` = client identifier,
   `cnf` = instance key) and preserves OpenID4VP's rule that `client_id` equals
   `sub`. No new artifact and no new claim are needed.

3. **Attester trust via the federation.** This specification defines what OpenID4VP
   left open: the attestation's `iss` is the provider's Entity Identifier, resolved
   through the Trust Chain to a Trust Anchor, requiring the provider entity type
   (and, where used, an accreditation Trust Mark). For offline and proximity flows
   the `trust_chain` JOSE header (per the Implementation Considerations for Offline
   Flows) allows validation against cached Trust Anchor keys without live resolution.

4. **Entitlement stays organizational; attestation may narrow it, never extend it.**
   The wallet resolves the `sub` entity and evaluates its registered metadata and
   entitlements (aligned with the registration direction of #56). The instance
   attestation asserts integrity and binding, and MAY additionally carry
   provider-asserted constraints that narrow the organizational entitlement for
   that specific instance (for example restricting requestable claims, transports,
   or assurance level, derived from the provider's own attestation of where and
   how the instance runs). The wallet evaluates the intersection of organizational
   entitlement and instance constraints, fail closed. An attestation can therefore
   never expand privileges, and a compromised provider can at worst reduce them;
   authorization authority remains with the federation. This mirrors
   metadata_policy semantics (superiors constrain, never expand) and RFC 8693
   scope narrowing.

This requires no normative change to OpenID4VP. We have implemented this pattern and
are now working with ecosystems that have this requirement in production ecosystems
at scale. We would be glad to contribute text.
items.title: Credential Verifier instances (POS terminals, mobile readers) have no trust model: define the Wallet Provider pattern for the verifier side

items.body:
Thank you for publishing the WISE proposal. Its focus on workload identity
lifecycle, credential/key state, trust material and posture is useful, especially
for AI-agent deployments. I have one boundary and privacy question that may be
worth making explicit before adoption.

The draft says that WISE addresses the non-human workload domain and that
workload identifiers should not encode information about the humans who manage
or operate workloads. It also uses a workload URI as the primary subject
identifier, and some events may carry credential identifiers, rotation links or
an artifact digest. These are operationally valuable, but together can create a
durable cross-domain correlation handle.

For an AI agent acting under a human or organisational delegation, could WISE
state explicitly that a WISE event:

1. asserts a change in **workload** credential, trust, lifecycle or posture;
2. does **not** assert the identity of a human or organisation on whose behalf
   the workload acts;
3. does **not** assert a mandate, consent, authorization for a particular
   action, or that an action occurred; and
4. is not by itself an action receipt or non-repudiation record?

Those claims normally need a distinct delegation credential and, where needed,
a separate action/evidence record. A compromised-workload event may be a strong
input to an authorization decision, but it should not create or extend a
workload's authority.

Could the privacy section also give deployment guidance for correlation data?
For example:

- explain when a globally stable WIMSE workload URI is required, versus when a
  Receiver-specific opaque/pairwise subject mapping is acceptable;
- apply purpose limitation and retention/deletion expectations to subject URI,
  `credential_id`, `previous_credential_id`, `new_credential_id`,
  `artifact_digest`, timestamps, and free-text administrative reasons;
- state that a Transmitter should disclose only the fields a particular
  authorized Receiver needs for the stated incident or lifecycle purpose; and
- include a non-normative two-Receiver example showing how the same workload
  can be signalled without unnecessarily giving unrelated Receivers a shared
  long-lived identifier.

This would preserve the important security properties already in the draft
(authorized event streams, `iat` freshness, `jti` replay detection, TLS/JWE)
while making a useful distinction: **workload posture is evidence relevant to a
decision, not a substitute for human/organisational authority or a record of an
action.**

## Why this is a focused contribution

- It follows the 2026-07-21 Shared Signals action item to review WISE and open
  issues using the `Workload identity` label.
- It does not ask WISE to standardize EUDIW, mandates or action receipts.
- It asks for scope and privacy guidance grounded in the current draft's
  workload-URI subjects, optional credential identifiers/artifact digest,
  authorization section and privacy considerations.

## Evidence checked

- WISE draft 02, sections “Scope”, “Subject Identifiers for Workload Events”,
  “Authorization”, “Privacy Considerations”:
  https://identitymonk.github.io/openid-wise/
- Shared Signals WG notes, 2026-07-21 (request for review/issues and adoption
  vote):
  https://github.com/openid/sharedsignals/wiki/WG-Meeting:-2026%E2%80%9007%E2%80%9021
- Local analytical boundary and test questions:
  `wise-shared-signals-watch.md`
items.title: Clarify the authority boundary and correlation guidance for WISE events involving AI agents

items.body: while reviewing the credential issuance flow, I may have noticed an architectural detail and wanted to get your thoughts to see if this could be considered a potential privacy leak. It seems that while successful credential responses are securely encrypted at the application layer (as opaque JWEs), error responses (like credential_request_denied) are explicitly required to be sent in plaintext. If a deployment uses a TLS-terminating intermediary (such as a CDN, Reverse Proxy or API Gateway), this intermediary can still easily deduce whether a user's request was approved or rejected just by looking at whether the response is encrypted or plaintext. I understand this might be an intended design choice for routing or debugging, but could this be considered a decision-state information leak in split-trust environments? I would much appreciate to hear your perspectives on this. Thank you in advance.
items.title: Potential side-channel at TLS-terminating intermediaries due to plaintext error responses?

items.body: I would like to ask for clarification upon a potential gap between the authorization session and the final holder key. Currently, there is no cryptographic term linking the End-User's authentication at the AS to the holder key presented later at the Credential Endpoint. This gap persists even when sender-constraining mechanisms like DPoP are strictly utilized. DPoP ensures the token presenter holds the DPoP key (K_{DPoP}), but it does not prove that the End-User authorized the specific credential binding key (K_H). For example, in a split-architecture wallet scenario (Section 13.4), a compromised backend holding a valid DPoP-bound token could unilaterally substitute its own holder key into the proofs parameter. The Issuer would then issue a valid credential bound to the attacker's key, completely unable to verify if this K_H belongs to the original authorized session. A way to prevent this substitution risk may be anchoring the intended holder key to the initial Authorization Request, similar to how the dpop_jkt parameter works in RFC 9449, creating an end-to-end commitment. Or do I miss some other details within the spec? Thank you in advance.
items.title: Potential key substitution risk due to missing session-key commitment ?

items.body:
## Problem statement

[connect-enterprise-extensions PR #5](https://github.com/openid/connect-enterprise-extensions/pull/5) introduces RP tenancy: the `aud_tenant` ID Token claim, the `client_tenant` authentication request parameter, and the `tenants` client registration metadata parameter. For a multi-tenant RP that shares a single `client_id` across its tenants, account identifier uniqueness becomes composite: `aud` + `aud_tenant` + `aud_sub` is unique within the RP, and the same `aud_sub` value may exist in different RP tenants.

Provider Commands currently treats `aud_sub` as a complete RP account key. Section 6: "Account Commands are executed on an RP Account identified in a Command Token by the `aud_sub` claim if provided by the RP during account resolution, or the `iss` and `sub` claims." There is no RP-tenant dimension anywhere in the protocol surface. For shared-client RPs this breaks:

1. **The closed claim set prohibits the disambiguator.** Section 5 allows only the listed baseline claims; `aud_tenant` cannot legally appear in a Command Token, and Tenant Commands prohibit `aud_sub` outright.
2. **Account addressing is ambiguous, with destructive consequences.** A Command Token carrying only `aud_sub` can match accounts in multiple RP tenants. The fallback key (`iss`, `tenant`, `sub`) is no better: the same OP account is routinely linked into more than one RP tenant (one user in two workspaces of the same SaaS app). Suspend, Archive, Delete, Invalidate, and Migrate are all defined against "the Account", singular. Executing them against the wrong tenant's account is exactly the cross-tenant confusion the Enterprise Extensions security considerations warn about. Note the claim mapping: the ID Token uniqueness triple `aud` + `aud_tenant` + `aud_sub` translates to `client_id` + `aud_tenant` + `aud_sub` in Command Tokens, since `aud` is the Command Endpoint here.
3. **Account Resolution is lossy.** Section 1.4.2 defines resolution as a bidirectional mapping where the OP learns a scalar `aud_sub`. The RP's identifier is now the pair (`aud_tenant`, `aud_sub`), and one (`iss`, `tenant`, `sub`) can map to several such pairs. No field in the Success Response (6.2) or audit responses lets the RP return `aud_tenant`, so the OP cannot store a well-formed mapping. `aud_sub_required` is incoherent for these RPs: requiring `aud_sub` without `aud_tenant` requires half a key.
4. **Audit Tenant streaming cannot disambiguate or dedupe.** Sections 7.4/7.6 key account-state events on `sub`. A shared-client RP with the same user in two RP tenants must emit two events with identical `sub` and possibly different states. OP reconciliation keyed on `sub` sees duplicate keys, and a returned `aud_sub` cannot be attributed to the right tenant.
5. **Tenant Commands fan out across RP tenants with no scoping.** Suspend/Archive/Delete/Invalidate Tenant (7.7-7.10) operate on all accounts for the OP tenant, which spans every RP tenant. An enterprise offboarding one workspace cannot scope `delete_tenant` to it. The single-valued `command_endpoint` client metadata (Section 10) rules out per-tenant endpoint routing as an escape hatch.
6. **Notifications are ambiguous.** Async result notifications (8.2) carry `sub` + `account_state` in a fresh RP-issued token with no HTTP correlation to the command, so a result for a `sub` that exists in multiple RP tenants cannot be attributed.
7. **Secondary: divergent claim definitions across three documents.** `tenant` and `aud_sub` are defined in OPC, EE, and ID-JAG (draft -04 now defines `tenant`, `aud_sub`, and `aud_tenant`) with drifting text and overlapping IANA registration plans. The IANA description here ("a logically isolated entity within the party identified by the `iss` of the token") already contradicts the Notification Token usage, where `iss` is the RP but `tenant` names an OP tenant. The EE PR additionally contains contradictory `aud_sub` uniqueness rules in normative text (unconditionally "unique within the context of the `client_id`", then pair-unique when `aud_tenant` is present), which needs resolution in the claim definitions, not only in the appendix.

The unique-client-per-tenant and single-tenant RP models are unaffected: `client_id` identifies the tenant and `aud_sub` stays unique per client. The damage is confined to, but complete for, the shared-client model that `aud_tenant` was created to serve. That model matters because backchannel flows (the IETF Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant, whose draft -04 now defines both `aud_sub` and `aud_tenant` in the grant with the same composite uniqueness rule) have no front-channel state (`redirect_uri`, `state`, cookies) to carry RP tenancy.

## Original driver: one tenancy vocabulary for ID Token and ID-JAG

`aud_tenant` originates in the need to unify two assertion flows under one set of tenancy claims: front-channel ID Tokens (Enterprise Extensions) and the backchannel [Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID-JAG)](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-04). ID-JAG adopted `aud_sub` from Enterprise Extensions, and draft -04 now defines `aud_tenant` in the grant with the same composite uniqueness rule, because every mechanism a front-channel RP uses to carry tenant context is unavailable on the backchannel. Provider Commands is the third leg of the same unification: it is the native provisioning and audit path in this specification suite for the tenant-qualified resolution map that ID-JAG consumes.

Scope qualifier: this driver applies to deployments where the Resource Authorization Server presents a shared issuer for all of its tenants. ID-JAG does not force that topology (a RAS may use tenant-specific issuers), but tenant-specific issuers recreate the per-tenant discovery, trust, and registration burden at every IdP that registration consolidation exists to remove, so the shared-issuer shape is the strategically important one.

### Worked scenario

Acme Corp runs its workforce identity on `https://idp.acme.example`. Acme uses two SaaS apps: WikiCo, a knowledge-base product where every team gets an isolated workspace, and ChatApp, a messaging product with an AI assistant. Acme has two WikiCo workspaces, `ws-eng` and `ws-legal`, created independently and bottom-up (engineering signed up in 2023, legal in 2025) before Acme's IdP relationship with WikiCo existed. That history is why Jane holds two unrelated member records: she signed up into each workspace separately, and WikiCo workspaces are independent account pools by design (the same model as per-workspace user records in Slack outside Enterprise Grid). There is no single source of truth for "Jane at WikiCo"; there is Jane-in-`ws-eng` and Jane-in-`ws-legal`.

WikiCo authenticates every customer through one central domain: `https://auth.wikico.example` is both its SSO front door and its authorization server issuer. When Acme's admin added WikiCo from the IdP's app catalog, that created exactly one client registration (`client_id: wikico-prod`), and both workspaces ride on it. This is the normal shape at SaaS scale: workspaces are created in WikiCo's own UI, long after and independent of the IdP integration, so one registration per workspace was never operationally on the table.

WikiCo member IDs are workspace-scoped, assigned from a per-workspace sequence:

| Person | IdP identity (`iss` + `sub`) | Workspace (`aud_tenant`) | WikiCo member ID (`aud_sub`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Jane | `idp.acme.example` / `00u1234` | `ws-eng` | `1042` |
| Jane | `idp.acme.example` / `00u1234` | `ws-legal` | `2210` |
| Raj | `idp.acme.example` / `00u5678` | `ws-legal` | `1042` |

Two things to notice: Jane's single IdP identity maps to two RP accounts, and the value `1042` names Jane in engineering but Raj in legal. `aud_sub` is a key only inside an `aud_tenant`; the pair is the identifier.

Front-channel SSO never noticed this. When Jane signs in to the legal workspace, her browser starts at `ws-legal.wikico.example`; WikiCo carries the workspace in `state` or a cookie on its own domain and routes the response itself, or falls back to asking the user. Front-channel flows have three escape hatches: RP-held browser state, per-tenant routing, and a live user who can be asked. The OP never needed to know workspaces existed.

Now the backchannel case. Jane asks ChatApp's assistant to summarize a document in the legal wiki. ChatApp (the ID-JAG Client) obtains a WikiCo API token in two legs:

```
Leg 1: ChatApp -> IdP token endpoint (RFC 8693)
  grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:token-exchange
  requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:id-jag
  audience=https://auth.wikico.example
  subject_token=<Jane's ID token or refresh token>

Leg 2: ChatApp -> WikiCo Resource Authorization Server
  grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer
  assertion=<ID-JAG: iss=idp.acme.example, sub=00u1234,
             aud=https://auth.wikico.example, client_id=...>
```

Every front-channel escape hatch is structurally absent:

- **No cookie.** Jane's user agent never touches `wikico.example` in this flow; the exchange may happen hours after SSO, minted off a refresh token, or from an autonomous agent with no human online.
- **No `state`, no `redirect_uri`.** Leg 2 is a token request, not an authorization request; nothing round-trips through a workspace-specific URL.
- **No user to ask.** A token endpoint cannot render a workspace picker; its only outputs are a token or an error, and the error goes to ChatApp's backend, not to Jane.
- **The `aud` carries no tenant signal.** It is WikiCo's single global AS issuer, shared by every workspace of every customer. It identifies WikiCo, not a workspace.

So the Resource Authorization Server holds an assertion saying "Jane, from Acme's IdP, for WikiCo" and must answer a question the token does not contain: which workspace? Without `aud_tenant` its options are all bad:

1. **Resolve by (`iss`, `sub`)**: two memberships match. Reject, and the feature fails for anyone in more than one workspace. Pick a default, and the assistant silently reads or writes the wrong workspace. Issue a cross-workspace token, and WikiCo breaks its own isolation model, since scopes and roles are workspace properties (Jane is an admin in `ws-eng`, read-only in `ws-legal`).
2. **Resolve by `aud_sub` alone** (the claim ID-JAG already has): `aud_sub=1042` matches Jane in engineering and Raj in legal. Resolve in the wrong tenant and the client is acting as a different human being. Without the tenant qualifier, `aud_sub` is not merely ambiguous; it can be confidently wrong.

With `aud_tenant`, the flow is deterministic end to end. ChatApp knows the target tenant from its task context and indicates it in the exchange request, the IdP validates it against WikiCo's registered `tenants` and issues the ID-JAG with `aud_tenant=ws-legal`, `aud_sub=2210`, and the Resource Authorization Server does one exact-match lookup and mints a token scoped to precisely that membership. (Coordination gap to note: ID-JAG -04 defines `aud_tenant` in the issued grant but its token-exchange request has no `client_tenant`-equivalent parameter; whether tenant selection rides on a tenant-specific `resource`, an `authorization_details` member, a new parameter, or client-bound policy is an open ID-JAG work item.)

The connection to this proposal: the IdP can only fill in `aud_tenant=ws-legal, aud_sub=2210` if it already holds the per-tenant mapping, and the backchannel gives it no way to learn that mapping lazily. Tenant-scoped account resolution is what provides it: a scoped Audit Tenant run against `ws-legal` teaches the IdP `00u1234 <-> (ws-legal, 2210)` unambiguously. Provider Commands builds the tenant-qualified resolution map; ID-JAG is the flow that consumes it where no front channel exists to compensate. Front-channel tenancy could stay out-of-band because the user agent carried it; backchannel tenancy must be in-band, in the token, because the token is the only thing that crosses the boundary.

## Proposed design

### Invariants

1. **One Command Token, one unambiguous scope.** An Account Command targets exactly one Account; a Tenant Command (except Metadata) targets exactly one (OP tenant, RP tenant) pair. Fan-out across RP tenants is always the OP issuing multiple commands, never the RP guessing.
2. **`sub` is unique within any command scope.** Events, responses, and OP-side reconciliation stay keyed on `sub` with no per-event disambiguation.
3. **RPs declare their account-identifier scope explicitly**, so the OP always knows which rules apply without probing or inference:
   - `account_identifier_scope=client` (the default when absent): `aud_sub` is unique within `client_id`. Covers single-tenant RPs, unique-client-per-tenant RPs, and multi-tenant RPs with a shared account store. Such an RP MAY still advertise `tenants` (as valid tenant contexts for routing, policy, or front-channel `aud_tenant`) without changing how accounts are addressed.
   - `account_identifier_scope=tenant`: accounts are partitioned into RP tenants; `aud_sub` is unique within (`client_id`, `aud_tenant`), and `aud_tenant` is required for account identification.

   Declaring `tenants` and declaring identifier scope are deliberately independent: tenancy as routing/policy context and tenancy as account partitioning are different properties, and only the latter changes command addressing.

All changes are additive and compatible with existing response shapes: `aud_tenant` never appears for `scope=client` RPs, and the Account State object introduced below matches today's response bodies. (A pre-existing OP cannot serve a `scope=tenant` RP without implementing the new claims; that is a new capability, not a regression.)

### Section-by-section changes

| Section | Change |
|---|---|
| 2.1 Claims | Add `aud_tenant` (defined by reference to Enterprise Extensions) |
| 2 (new 2.3) | Define the Account State object once |
| 4 (new 4.5) | New error `aud_tenant_required` |
| 5 Command Token | Both baselines gain OPTIONAL `aud_tenant` |
| 6 Account Commands | Rewrite the account-identification rule; normative manager-of-record authorization check; responses become Account State objects |
| 7 Tenant Commands | Scoping rule (defined for `scope=tenant` only); streaming events become Account State objects; fix examples |
| 7.2 Metadata Response | `account_identifier_scope` member; `tenants` member filtered by the requesting OP tenant's authority |
| 8 Notifications | Async results carry the Account State object, echoing `aud_tenant` |
| 10 (new subsection) | Explicit identifier-scope declaration and the two account models |
| 14 IANA | One definition and one registration per claim, coordinated across OPC/EE/ID-JAG |

**2.1, new claim:**

> `aud_tenant`: Identifier of the RP tenant that contains the Account, as defined in OpenID Connect Enterprise Extensions. The value is opaque to the OP and is stable and unique within the context of the `client_id`. When present together with `aud_sub`, the pair identifies the Account within the RP.

Provider Commands references the coordinated definition (see the IANA note below) rather than defining or registering the claim independently.

**New 2.3, Account State object:**

> An Account State object is a JSON object describing one Account at the RP. It is the payload for Account Command responses, `account-state` events, and asynchronous result notifications.
>
> - `sub` REQUIRED: the Subject Identifier of the Account at the OP.
> - `account_state` REQUIRED: one of `unknown`, `active`, `suspended`, `archived`, or a temporary `*_pending` state.
> - `aud_tenant` OPTIONAL: the RP tenant containing the Account. When the corresponding Command Token contained `aud_tenant`, the value MUST be identical.
> - `aud_sub` OPTIONAL: the RP's identifier for the Account.
> - `last_access` OPTIONAL: NumericDate of last account access.
> - `authentication_provider` OPTIONAL: see 2.1.
>
> An Account State object MAY include additional Claims for the Account where the command's section specifies.

Per-site requirement levels stay at the reuse sites (e.g., "`aud_sub` MUST be included if the RP set `aud_sub_required`" remains in 6.2; retained-claims requirements remain in the audit sections). The four near-duplicate property lists (6.2, 6.3, 6.11, 7.4/8.2) become one-line references to this object.

**New 4.5, Tenant Scope Required error:**

> If the RP has declared `account_identifier_scope=tenant` and the Command Token does not include an `aud_tenant` claim, the RP MUST return an HTTP 400 Bad Request and include the `error` parameter with the value `aud_tenant_required`. The OP obtains the RP's tenant identifiers from the `tenants` client metadata or the Metadata Response and retries the Command scoped to a single RP tenant.

One error code covers both Account and Tenant Commands. An unrecognized `aud_tenant` value is `invalid_request` with an `error_description`.

**5, baselines:**

- Account Command baseline: OPTIONAL becomes `aud_sub`, `aud_tenant`.
- Tenant Command baseline: add OPTIONAL `aud_tenant` (`sub`, `aud_sub` stay PROHIBITED).
- Metadata Command (7.1) exception: `aud_tenant` PROHIBITED. The Metadata exchange describes the client-wide relationship and is the bootstrap surface where the OP learns the tenant list, so it stays unscoped.
- An OP MUST NOT include `aud_tenant` in Command Tokens for an RP that has not declared `account_identifier_scope=tenant`; an RP that receives it anyway MAY reject the token as `invalid_request`.

**6, account identification rule (replaces the current sentence):**

> Account Commands are executed on a single RP Account. The Account is identified by the `aud_sub` claim when present, or otherwise by the `iss`, `tenant`, and `sub` claims; in both cases, when the `aud_tenant` claim is present, identification is within the RP tenant it names. For RPs declaring `account_identifier_scope=tenant` (see §10.x), Command Tokens for Account Commands MUST include `aud_tenant`; the RP rejects Command Tokens without it per Section 4.5.
>
> Identification does not imply authorization. Regardless of how the Account is identified, and even when a valid `aud_sub` is supplied, the RP MUST verify that the requesting `iss` and `tenant` are authorized to manage the targeted Account (and, when applicable, the RP tenant named by `aud_tenant`) before executing the Command, and MUST return `access_denied` otherwise. A correct native identifier, guessed or stale, is not a grant of authority.

6.2 returns HTTP 200 with an Account State object; 6.3 returns HTTP 409 with an Account State object extended with `error: incompatible_state`; 6.11 returns an Account State object plus retained Claims. Extend `aud_sub_required` with one sentence instead of adding a metadata member: "For RPs declaring `account_identifier_scope=tenant`, `aud_sub_required` indicates the RP requires both `aud_sub` and `aud_tenant`."

**7, Tenant Commands intro:**

> When the Command Token includes `aud_tenant`, the Command executes only within the RP tenant it identifies. RPs declaring `account_identifier_scope=tenant` MUST reject Tenant Commands other than the Metadata Command that omit `aud_tenant` per Section 4.5.
>
> `aud_tenant`-scoped Tenant Commands are defined only for `account_identifier_scope=tenant`. For a shared account store (`scope=client`), a tenant-scoped lifecycle command is semantically ambiguous (deleting the shared account damages other tenants; removing one membership is not account deletion), so this proposal does not define it; membership lifecycle over shared stores is explicitly future work.

**7.4, Streaming Response:**

> The `data` parameter of the `account-state` event MUST contain an Account State object. All events in a Streaming Response are scoped to the `iss`, `tenant`, and, when present, `aud_tenant` of the Command Token; each `account-state` event describes a distinct Account, and `sub` values are unique within a Streaming Response.

The uniqueness sentence is the payoff of scoping: it holds for `scope=client` RPs today and for `scope=tenant` RPs because the stream is per tenant pair. Events need no per-event `aud_tenant`; it is implied by the request.

**7.5 example, corrected** (the current example also omits the REQUIRED `tenant` claim):

```json
{
  "iss": "https://op.example.org",
  "aud": "https://rp.example.net/command",
  "client_id": "s6BhdRkqt3",
  "iat": 1734003000,
  "exp": 1734003060,
  "jti": "bWJz",
  "command": "audit_tenant",
  "tenant": "ff6e7c96",
  "aud_tenant": "acme-corp-tenant-id"
}
```

**7.7 through 7.10:** for `scope=tenant` RPs, e.g. "the RP MUST suspend all Accounts in the active state for the Tenant identified by the `tenant` Claim, within the RP tenant identified by the `aud_tenant` Claim when present." For `scope=tenant` RPs this bounds the blast radius of `delete_tenant` to one workspace, which the current text cannot express; for `scope=client` RPs these commands remain unscoped as today (see the Tenant Commands intro above).

**7.2, Metadata Response:**

> `account_identifier_scope` (OPTIONAL): JSON string, `client` or `tenant`. Declares the scope within which the RP's `aud_sub` values are unique. When absent, the value is `client`.
>
> `tenants` (OPTIONAL): JSON array of RP tenant identifiers for this `client_id`, as defined in OpenID Connect Enterprise Extensions, filtered to those the requesting `iss` and `tenant` are authorized to manage. RPs declaring `account_identifier_scope=tenant` MUST include `tenants`.

The filtering requirement is both least-privilege and privacy: an unfiltered `tenants` array would disclose the RP's customer list to any OP holding a registration. `tenants` itself reuses EE PR #5's registration metadata (7.2 already allows any registration metadata in the response); `account_identifier_scope` is the one genuinely new member, and it exists because tenancy-as-context and tenancy-as-account-partition are independent properties that must not be inferred from one another. Tenant churn composes with existing machinery: RP adds a customer, sends the existing `metadata_change` notification, OP reruns Metadata and audits the new tenant.

**8.2, Notifications:**

> If the notification is for the result of an asynchronous Account Command, the members of the Account State object for the Account are included as claims. When the Command Token of the asynchronous Command included `aud_tenant`, the notification MUST include the same `aud_tenant` value.

The echo requirement matters because a notification is a fresh RP-issued token with no HTTP correlation to the command.

**New 10.x, RP Account Identifier Scope:**

> RPs whose account identifiers are unique within the `client_id` use the protocol exactly as defined elsewhere in this specification; the `aud_tenant` claim and `aud_tenant_required` error do not apply to them. This includes single-tenant RPs, RPs with a unique `client_id` per tenant, and multi-tenant RPs with a shared account store.
>
> An RP declares the scope of its account identifiers with the `account_identifier_scope` metadata value:
>
> 1. **`client`** (default when absent): `aud_sub` values are unique within the `client_id`. The RP MAY still advertise `tenants` and use `aud_tenant` in ID Tokens for routing or policy; this does not change how Commands identify Accounts.
> 2. **`tenant`**: Accounts are partitioned into RP tenants, and `aud_sub` values are unique within the combination of `client_id` and `aud_tenant`. The RP MUST advertise its tenant identifiers (filtered by requester authority) and MUST reject Command Tokens that omit `aud_tenant`, except the Metadata Command, with the `aud_tenant_required` error.
>
> An RP that declares (or defaults to) `account_identifier_scope=client` MUST ensure any `aud_sub` values it returns are unique within the `client_id`.
>
> The scope of account identifiers is determined by the RP's data model, not by the presence of tenants: an RP with a central account store and a single `aud_sub` per user is `client`-scoped regardless of how many tenants it serves. Such an RP enforces tenant boundaries by authorizing Commands against the Account's managing OP (`iss` and `tenant`), and represents tenant membership as claims rather than command scope.

An RP either guarantees client-wide uniqueness (and the spec works unchanged) or declares `tenant` scope (and gets scoped addressing). There is no third state, no inference from `tenants`, and the OP determines the model from metadata alone.

**14, IANA:** each of `tenant`, `aud_sub`, and `aud_tenant` needs exactly one authoritative definition, one semantic contract, and one IANA registration across the three documents that currently touch them (OPC proposes registering `tenant`; ID-JAG -04 defines all three and registers under IETF change control; EE defines all three with its IANA section incomplete). Which document owns which claim is an explicit OIDF/IETF coordination decision to be made before any of the three advances; this proposal takes no position beyond requiring that OPC reference, not redefine, whatever the coordinated definitions are.

### End-to-end flow (shared-client RP)

1. RP registers `client_id` with `command_endpoint` (and `tenants`, if known at registration).
2. OP sends Metadata Command (unscoped). RP returns `commands_supported`, `account_identifier_scope: "tenant"`, `tenants: ["acme-corp-tenant-id", "widgets-inc-tenant-id"]` (filtered to the tenants this OP tenant manages), `aud_sub_required`.
3. OP runs Audit Tenant once per (OP tenant, RP tenant) pair. Each stream is internally `sub`-unique and every returned `aud_sub` unambiguously belongs to that pair.
4. Lifecycle commands carry `aud_tenant` (plus `aud_sub` once resolved). One command, one account, singular response.
5. RP onboards a new customer: `metadata_change`, then Metadata Command, then audit the new tenant.
6. An enterprise offboards one workspace: `delete_tenant` with `aud_tenant`, touching nothing else.

## Impact

- **`scope=client` RPs (single-tenant, client per tenant, or shared account store): no new wire fields.** No new claims received, no new errors to emit or handle, no metadata required (`account_identifier_scope` defaults to `client`), no response shape changes. The one new obligation (client-wide `aud_sub` uniqueness) codifies what they already do; conformance and test costs remain, but no protocol behavior changes. The escape-hatch sentence in 10.x lets this population stop reading.
- **Additive and compatible with existing response shapes.** Existing 6.2 responses such as `{"account_state": "active", "sub": "..."}` are already valid Account State objects; the object introduces no renames. Note the honest limit: a pre-existing OP cannot interoperate with a `scope=tenant` RP without implementing the new claims; that is a new capability, not a regression.
- **`scope=tenant` RPs** implement `aud_tenant` scope validation, the `aud_tenant_required` error, the manager-of-record authorization check, and authority-filtered `tenants` advertisement. This is the population that currently has no conformant option at all.
- **OPs supporting `scope=tenant` RPs** discover tenant lists, audit per tenant pair, store `aud_tenant` in the resolution map, and fan out cross-tenant actions explicitly.
- **Spec text shrinks in places**: four duplicated response property lists collapse into one Account State object definition, ending drift between them (they already disagree slightly).
- **Coordination**: one definition, one semantic contract, and one IANA registration per claim across OPC, EE, and ID-JAG, with ownership decided explicitly (see 14 above); EE's contradictory `aud_sub` uniqueness rules fixed in normative text; ID-JAG's request-side tenant selection defined.

## Tradeoffs

Costs of the proposal, and what each buys:

| Cost | What it buys |
|---|---|
| One new claim, one new error, one new metadata member, one new section | Shared-client tenant-partitioned RPs become conformant with a correct composite key; without this they cannot use Provider Commands once EE ships |
| Normative dependency on the coordinated EE/ID-JAG claim definitions | One definition and one registration per claim; resolves the existing `tenant` multi-definition and IANA overlap |
| OP orchestration grows (tenant discovery, per-pair audits, scoped resolution map) | Every audit stream is `sub`-unique and every learned `aud_sub` is bound to a tenant pair; reconciliation logic stays keyed on `sub` |
| Cross-tenant actions take N explicit commands (e.g., invalidating a compromised account everywhere) | No RP guessing on destructive operations; singular responses stay singular; wrong-tenant suspend/delete becomes structurally impossible |
| Tenant-list freshness is a moving part | Handled by the existing `metadata_change` notification loop; no new notification types or endpoints |
| Conformance suites cover two RP models | The model is deterministic from metadata, so each RP is tested against exactly one |

The alternatives considered and rejected:

- **Per-event `aud_tenant` tagging instead of scoped audits**: keeps single giant streams but pushes disambiguation into every event, every response, and every OP reconciliation key. More invasive, not less.
- **Per-tenant Command Endpoints**: `command_endpoint` is single-valued, and EE explicitly forbids the analogous URL-sniffing pattern for `redirect_uri`.
- **Do nothing**: correct only until EE ships `aud_tenant`; after that, `aud_sub` silently stops being a key for shared-client RPs and the failure mode is destructive commands against the wrong tenant's account.

## Non-goals

Kept out to hold the change minimal: the SSE transport and `Last-Event-Id` resumption are untouched (per-tenant scoping shrinks stream sizes, which softens that problem independently); the audit claim echo stays mandatory as today; Metadata remains client-wide (per-RP-tenant capability variation is not modeled); nothing on the ID Token side changes (that is EE's surface).

## References

- Rendered spec: https://openid.github.io/openid-provider-commands/main.html
- Enterprise Extensions PR introducing RP tenancy: https://github.com/openid/connect-enterprise-extensions/pull/5
- Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant -04 (defines `aud_sub` and `aud_tenant` in the grant): https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/draft-ietf-oauth-identity-assertion-authz-grant-04

## Revisions

**2026-07-30**, in response to review feedback (including [the discussion below](https://github.com/openid/openid-provider-commands/issues/33#issuecomment-5004342176)):

- **Decoupled account-identifier scope from tenant advertisement.** New `account_identifier_scope = client | tenant` metadata (default `client`) replaces the earlier inference "advertises `tenants` implies partitioned accounts". A shared-account-store RP can now advertise `tenants` for routing or policy while keeping a globally unique `aud_sub`, and Maintain runs once against its single record. This directly addresses the central-account-pool case.
- **Added a normative manager-of-record authorization check** to Account Commands: identification (even by valid `aud_sub`) never implies authorization.
- **`tenants` disclosure is filtered** by the requesting OP tenant's authority (least privilege, and avoids leaking the RP's customer list).
- **Restricted `aud_tenant`-scoped Tenant Commands to `scope=tenant` RPs**; membership lifecycle over shared stores is named as future work rather than implied.
- **Corrected the ID-JAG framing**: draft -04 now defines `aud_tenant` in the grant; the shared-issuer RAS topology is strategically favored, not protocol-mandated; the missing request-side tenant-selection parameter is flagged as an ID-JAG coordination item.
- **Softened claims**: "additive and compatible" rather than "wire compatible"; "no new wire fields" rather than "zero cost"; IANA ownership left to explicit OIDF/IETF coordination rather than assigned to EE.
- **Worked scenario** now explains why per-workspace identifiers exist (independent bottom-up workspace creation preceding the enterprise relationship).
items.title: RP tenancy (aud_tenant) breaks account identification: scoped commands and a shared Account State object

**Impact observed:** while implementing an SSF receiver and running it against the official conformance suite for certification, this ambiguity caused a real, confusing failure. Our schema for the stream configuration object declared optional fields as "string or absent" (a literal reading of OPTIONAL), which is what most runtime validators (zod, Pydantic, JSON Schema, etc.) produce by default. The transmitter's stream-create response included "description": null instead of omitting the key. Our validator rejected the response as malformed and returned a 500 — even though the transmitter had, in fact, already created the stream successfully. Because our error made it look like the create had failed, we tried again, and the second attempt was rejected with a 409 ("Only one stream allowed for receiver", OIDSSF-8.1.1.1) because the first stream silently existed already. This required manually discovering and deleting the orphaned stream before recreating it correctly. The root cause was purely the null-vs-absent ambiguity: a strictly-typed but spec-compliant receiver implementation broke against the reference transmitter's own output.

**Where:** SSF 1.0 §7.1.1 defines the JSON shape of the stream configuration resource, including several OPTIONAL fields (e.g. description, iss, aud, events_supported). The spec text doesn't state whether an implementation may represent an unset OPTIONAL field as an explicit JSON null, or whether it must omit the key entirely.

 **Observed transmitter behavior:** the official conformance suite (demo.certification.openid.net, suite version 5.2.0) returns explicit null for unset optional fields on stream creation (e.g. "description": null) rather than omitting the key.

Why this matters generally: JSON distinguishes an absent key from an explicit null value, and RFC 8259 doesn't mandate treating them as equivalent. Any receiver that types OPTIONAL fields as "string or absent" will fail to parse a spec-compliant-looking response from the reference transmitter itself.

**Suggested fix:** add clarifying text to §7.1.1 (and any other section defining JSON object shapes with OPTIONAL fields):

Receivers MUST treat an explicit JSON null value as equivalent to the field being absent for all OPTIONAL fields. Transmitters SHOULD omit OPTIONAL fields with no value rather than serializing them as null.
items.title: SSF 1.0 §7.1.1: spec doesn't clarify whether receivers must accept null for unset OPTIONAL fields in the stream configuration object

items.body:
While reviewing the batch credential issuance flow, I may have come across a logical contradiction between Section 8.3 and Section 14.6, regarding the maximum number of credentials that can be issued per request. 

Section 8.3 strictly limits the output by stating that "_each key provided by the Wallet is used to bind to, at most, one Credential_". 

However, Section 14.6 contradicts this upper bound by stating that the issuer determines the number of issued credentials "_regardless of number of proofs/keys contained in the proofs parameter_". 

This may cause an ambiguous situation: 
if an issuer follows Section 14.6 and returns more credentials than the provided keys, it forces the wallet to either reuse keys across credentials or accept unbound credentials, which directly violates the strict "at most one Credential" rule in Section 8.3.
items.title: Logical Contradiction between 8.3 and 14.6 on Batch Cardinality

# HAIP 1.1: "certificate signing the request" is a copy-paste artifact in three clauses that do not involve a request

**Spec / revision:** OpenID4VC High Assurance Interoperability Profile 1.1 (draft)
**Pinned source:** https://github.com/openid/OpenID4VC-HAIP/blob/8f45ca301e822d4abe944d1085d60d7cd015087f/1.1/openid4vc-high-assurance-interoperability-profile-1_1.md

## Summary

The sentence

> The X.509 certificate signing **the request** MUST NOT be self-signed.

appears verbatim in several clauses. In two of them it is correct, because a *request* is genuinely what is being signed (the signed key attestation, and the signed OpenID4VP authorization request). In **three** other clauses the same sentence was copied without adapting the noun, and the object being signed is **not** a request:

1. **Signed Credential Issuer Metadata** — the thing signed is the *Issuer Metadata*.
2. **SD-JWT VC Status List Token** — the thing signed is the *Status List Token*.
3. **SD-JWT VC issuer signature (key resolution)** — the thing signed is the *SD-JWT VC* itself.

In all three, the phrase "the request" has **no antecedent** in its paragraph — none of these paragraphs mention or involve a request. The requirement (no self-signed signer certificate) is presumably intended, but the wording is wrong and confusing for implementers and conformance testers, who must guess which "request" is meant.

The fix is editorial only: replace "the request" with the object that each clause actually signs. No normative change is intended.

This is not a 1.1 regression: all three occurrences are inherited **unchanged from the final published HAIP 1.0**, with byte-identical wording (see "Provenance" below).

## Locations to change

Section references use the heading title and its stable `{#anchor}`; the current text is quoted exactly as it appears at the pinned commit.

---

### 1. Issuer Metadata — `## Issuer Metadata {#issuer-metadata}`

(within "OpenID for Verifiable Credential Issuance")

**Current text:**

> Key resolution to validate the signed Issuer Metadata MUST be supported using the `x5c` JOSE header parameter as defined in [@!RFC7515]. In this case, the X.509 certificate of the trust anchor MUST NOT be included in the `x5c` JOSE header of the signed request. The X.509 certificate signing the request MUST NOT be self-signed.

**Proposed text:**

> Key resolution to validate the signed Issuer Metadata MUST be supported using the `x5c` JOSE header parameter as defined in [@!RFC7515]. In this case, the X.509 certificate of the trust anchor MUST NOT be included in the `x5c` JOSE header of the signed Issuer Metadata. The X.509 certificate signing the Issuer Metadata MUST NOT be self-signed.

> Note: in this paragraph the preceding sentence has the same defect — "the `x5c` JOSE header of the signed request" also refers to the signed Issuer Metadata, not a request. Both occurrences are corrected in the proposal above.

---

### 2. Status List Token — `## IETF SD-JWT VC Profile {#sd-jwt-vc}`

(the bullet on the Status List Token, within "OpenID4VC Credential Format Profiles")

**Current text:**

> * The public key used to validate the signature on the Status List Token defined in [I-D.ietf-oauth-status-list] MUST be included in the `x5c` JOSE header of the Token. The X.509 certificate of the trust anchor MUST NOT be included in the `x5c` JOSE header of the Status List Token. The X.509 certificate signing the request MUST NOT be self-signed.

**Proposed text:**

> * The public key used to validate the signature on the Status List Token defined in [I-D.ietf-oauth-status-list] MUST be included in the `x5c` JOSE header of the Token. The X.509 certificate of the trust anchor MUST NOT be included in the `x5c` JOSE header of the Status List Token. The X.509 certificate signing the Status List Token MUST NOT be self-signed.

---

### 3. SD-JWT VC issuer signature — `### Issuer identification and key resolution to validate an issued Credential {#issuer-key-resolution}`

(subsection of "IETF SD-JWT VC Profile")

**Current text:**

> This specification mandates the support for X.509 certificate-based key resolution to validate the issuer signature of an SD-JWT VC. This MUST be supported by all entities (Issuer, Wallet, Verifier). The SD-JWT VC MUST contain the credential issuer's signing certificate along with a trust chain in the `x5c` JOSE header parameter as described in section 3.5 of [@!I-D.ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc]. The X.509 certificate of the trust anchor MUST NOT be included in the `x5c` JOSE header of the SD-JWT VC. The X.509 certificate signing the request MUST NOT be self-signed.

**Proposed text:**

> This specification mandates the support for X.509 certificate-based key resolution to validate the issuer signature of an SD-JWT VC. This MUST be supported by all entities (Issuer, Wallet, Verifier). The SD-JWT VC MUST contain the credential issuer's signing certificate along with a trust chain in the `x5c` JOSE header parameter as described in section 3.5 of [@!I-D.ietf-oauth-sd-jwt-vc]. The X.509 certificate of the trust anchor MUST NOT be included in the `x5c` JOSE header of the SD-JWT VC. The X.509 certificate signing the SD-JWT VC MUST NOT be self-signed.

---

## Occurrences that are already correct (no change needed)

For completeness, so the fix is not applied too broadly:

- **`### Key Attestation {#key-attestation}`** — "The X.509 certificate signing **the key attestation** MUST NOT be self-signed." The noun was already adapted correctly here.
- **`# OpenID for Verifiable Presentations {#openid-for-verifiable-presentations}`** — "For signed requests, ... The X.509 certificate signing **the request** MUST NOT be self-signed." Here the object genuinely is a (signed authorization) request, so "the request" is correct.

These two are almost certainly the origin of the template sentence that was then copied into the three clauses above.

## Provenance: already present in HAIP 1.0

All three defective occurrences already exist in the **final, published HAIP 1.0**, with wording byte-identical to 1.1 (verified against `https://openid.net/specs/openid4vc-high-assurance-interoperability-profile-1_0.html`). The published 1.0 rendering assigns them these section numbers:

| # | HAIP 1.0 section | HAIP 1.1 heading / anchor |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | **4.1 Issuer Metadata** | Issuer Metadata `{#issuer-metadata}` |
| 2 | **6.1 IETF SD-JWT VC Profile** (Status List Token bullet) | IETF SD-JWT VC Profile `{#sd-jwt-vc}` |
| 3 | **6.1.1 Issuer identification and key resolution to validate an issued Credential** | `{#issuer-key-resolution}` |

In each of these three 1.0 sections the sentence reads exactly "The X.509 certificate signing the request MUST NOT be self-signed." So this is a long-standing editorial defect carried forward into the 1.1 draft, not something newly introduced in 1.1 — worth fixing in 1.1 rather than perpetuating it further.

## Related issues (checked 2026-07-15)

No open issue targets this editorial "the request" wording defect directly; this is not a duplicate. Adjacent open issues, and how this one differs:

- **#372 — "Clarification about trust anchor limitations"** (open): discusses the *same paragraph* as Location 3 (§6.1.1), and quotes "...signing the request MUST NOT be self-signed" verbatim, but only as a *substantive/normative* question — whether a leaf or self-signed certificate may serve as a trust anchor (incl. the EUDIW PID / ETSI TS 119 412-6 self-certified case). No participant there flags "the request" as a wording error. **This issue is purely editorial and deliberately does not touch the normative question raised in #372.**
- **#368 — "text around self-signed certificates / excluding trust anchor not present in wallet attestation section"** (open): the same boilerplate family, but the opposite defect — it notes the trust-anchor-exclusion and not-self-signed sentences are *missing* from the Wallet Attestation section and should be added for consistency. Orthogonal to this issue (missing text vs. wrong noun), though both aim at normalizing the `x5c` / self-signed boilerplate across sections and could be handled together.
- **#371 — "Discovery of public key / certificates of Verifier by Wallet"** (open): quotes the §5 (OpenID for Verifiable Presentations) occurrence, which is one of the *correct* ones — there "the request" genuinely denotes a signed authorization request. Not affected by this fix.

For context, this boilerplate originates from the closed issues **#236** ("Clarify that x509_hash certificates shall not be self-signed certificates") and **#237** ("Trust anchor certificate shall not be included in the `x5c`"), which introduced the sentence for the OID4VP signed request; it was subsequently copied into the other `x5c` clauses, which is how "the request" propagated into sections that involve no request.
items.title: HAIP 1.1: "certificate signing the request" is a copy-paste artifact in three clauses that do not involve a request

## Summary

Add byte-identical conformance test vectors for the denial-binding `binding_hash` construction, so an independently implemented PDP and Access Request Service have a pass/fail target instead of a prose-only specification.

## Background

`binding-token-integrity` pins the hashed denial-binding form by recomputation over a JCS ([RFC 8785](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8785)) serialized JSON object plus SHA-256. That is correct, but prose-pinned canonicalization is exactly where independently implemented parties quietly diverge (the field set, nesting, and how `binding_context_members` selects the hashed context members).

Raised in PR #532 review, where a reviewer offered to contribute vectors already validated byte-for-byte across TypeScript, Python, and Go.

## Scope

Vectors for:

- **Single-item `binding_hash`:** `base64url(SHA-256(JCS({"subject": <Subject>, "resource": <Resource>, "action": <Action>, "context": <authz-relevant Context>})))`, with `subject.properties.act` removed.
- **Bulk `binding_hash`:** the `{"subject": <Subject>, "items": [{"resource": <Resource>, "action": <Action>}, ...], "context": <authz-relevant Context>}` form, preserving bound item order.
- **`binding_context_members` selection:** which context members feed the hash (the subtlest part, and the one most worth a vector).
- **Edge cases:** absent vs `null` members, number canonicalization, array ordering, and an empty authorization-relevant context.

## Where

An interop test-vectors location, or a draft appendix. TBD.

## Depends on

Freezing the `binding_hash` field object (currently specified in `binding-token-integrity`); tracks PR #532.
items.title: Conformance vectors for binding_hash (JCS + SHA-256)

Section 8.2.1 (Paginated Requests) says:

> Furthermore, the PDP MUST declare support for the corresponding capability URN in its `supported_capabilities` metadata (Section 9.1.2).

There is no `supported_capabilities` metadata member. Section 9.1.2, which this sentence itself cross-references, defines the member as `capabilities`, and that is the name registered in the PDP Metadata Registry (Section 12.3). `supported_capabilities` appears nowhere else in the document, and it is also present in the published version.
