_From a security review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04** against [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) and [draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics-update-03](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics-update-03.html) (the in-progress extension of BCP 240)._

The aggregated claims topology is exactly the brokered-OAuth setting of security-topics-update §2.4: the OP is the **broker**, RPs are the **downstream clients**, and CPs are the **upstream authorization servers**. The Setup Phase deliberately obtains one broad upstream grant and reuses it for many downstream RPs — the shared-consent pattern §2.4 warns about.

Of the two countermeasures, per-client registration (§2.4.2.1 — registering every RP at every CP) is deliberately not used here, and for good reason: it would defeat the design and the privacy benefit that CPs do not learn which RPs the user visits (see #12). That makes the broker-side consent screen (§2.4.2.2) the load-bearing countermeasure. The draft's Subject Granting section already requires per-request consent, but two gaps remain against §2.4.2.2:

1. It requires the OP to "show the Subject what is being requested from the RP", but it does not explicitly require the consent screen to **identify the requesting RP**.
2. Nothing prohibits the OP from skipping the consent dialogue on the basis of consent previously given to a **different** RP.

**Proposed fix**
- Require the OP to identify the requesting RP on the consent screen (name and `client_id`-linked metadata), in addition to the requested claims and the `policy_uri` link.
- Require the OP to obtain consent per RP; the OP MAY remember a consent decision for a given RP, but the OP MUST NOT skip the consent dialogue based on consent given to a different RP (§2.4.2.2).
- State explicitly (Security Considerations) that per-client registration at the CP (§2.4.2.1) is not used, and why the broker-side consent screen is the chosen countermeasure.
items.title: [Security] The OP is a broker: shared-consent requirements for per-RP consent (security-topics-update §2.4)

items.body:
_From a security review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04** against [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) and [draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics-update-03](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics-update-03.html) (the in-progress extension of BCP 240)._

The Setup Phase is vulnerable to cross-user OAuth session fixation (security-topics-update §2.3): an attacker starts the Setup Phase in **their own** OP session and gets the victim to complete the authentication and consent at the CP (e.g. by delivering the authorization URL or completing the flow on a shared/other device). The CP then issues tokens for the **victim's** CP account, which the OP binds to the **attacker's** OP account. From then on, the attacker can present the victim's signed identity claims to RPs as their own.

Note that the trust-model provision in #1 ("bind the UserInfo access token to the account of the OP that started the authentication request") does not stop this — the attacker *is* the account that started the request. The missing control is same-user completion.

**Proposed fix**
- Require the OP to ensure that the Setup Phase flow initiated by one user is completed by the same user: the OP MUST bind its authorization request (`state`/PKCE) to the initiating user's session and MUST verify that binding when it receives the authorization response, per §2.3.2.
- Recommend that the OP compare the `sub` returned by the CP against any `sub` it has previously stored for that user–CP pairing, and treat a change as a signal requiring re-verification rather than silent rebinding.
items.title: [Security] Setup Phase session fixation binds the victim's CP claims to the attacker's OP account (security-topics-update §2.3)

items.body:
_From a security review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04** against [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) and [draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics-update-03](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics-update-03.html) (the in-progress extension of BCP 240)._

The OP maintains parallel OAuth client connections to many CPs. If the OP processes authorization responses on a shared redirection endpoint without binding each response to the specific CP connection it belongs to, a malicious CP — or an attacker able to register as a CP — can cause a response from one connection context to be consumed in another (Cross-toolkit OAuth Account Takeover, security-topics-update §2.2). In this document's setting, the consequence is that tokens or claims from the wrong CP connection get bound into a user's claims store.

§2.2.2 requires the client to form a connection context identifier, issue per-context distinct redirection URIs incorporating it, and verify on each authorization response that the context identifier in the redirection URI matches the one stored in the user's session, aborting on mismatch. The RFC 9700 §4.4.2 mix-up countermeasures (see #2) may substitute only under the conditions listed there (no implicit grant, issuer-coupled endpoint resolution).

**Proposed fix**
- Require the OP to bind every authorization response to the intended CP connection: the OP MUST use per-CP-connection distinct redirection URIs carrying a context identifier, MUST verify that identifier against the user's session, and MUST abort the flow on mismatch — or the OP MUST satisfy the substitution conditions of §2.2.2 together with `iss` validation (see #2).
items.title: [Security] Per-CP connection context binding for the multi-CP OP (COAT, security-topics-update §2.2)

items.body:
_From a security review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04** against [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) and [draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics-update-03](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics-update-03.html) (the in-progress extension of BCP 240)._

The OP authenticates as a client to **many** CPs. If it uses signature-based client authentication (`private_key_jwt`, JWT bearer assertions) — as proposed in #4 — the audience injection attack of security-topics-update §2.1 applies: a malicious CP can steer the audience value of the OP's authentication assertion (e.g. via attacker-influenced endpoint URLs in its metadata) so that the assertion is also valid at an honest CP, letting the attacker impersonate the OP there.

Per §2.1.2, clients that interact with more than one authorization server using signature-based client authentication MUST employ one of the defined countermeasures.

**Proposed fix**
- Require the OP, when it authenticates to a CP with a signature-based method, to set the audience of the assertion to either the CP's issuer identifier (which the OP MUST retrieve and validate per OIDC Discovery / RFC 8414) or the exact endpoint URI the assertion is sent to, as the **sole** audience value (§2.1.2.1 / §2.1.2.2).
- Recommend that the OP use distinct key material per CP as defense in depth (§2.1.2.3).
items.title: [Security] Audience injection on signature-based OP client authentication at CPs (security-topics-update §2.1)

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The Registration Phase says the OP MUST register `userinfo_signed_response_alg`, described as "Signing algorithm **supported by the Claims Provider**". It is the algorithm the OP *requests* the CP to use for its signed UserInfo responses (chosen from what the CP supports). The description inverts the direction.

**Proposed fix**
- Reword: "The JWS algorithm that the OP requests the CP to use when signing UserInfo responses. The OP MUST set the value to one of the values the CP advertises. The OP MUST NOT set the value to `none`."
items.title: [Editorial] Registration Phase description of userinfo_signed_response_alg inverts the direction

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The Abstract says "section 5.6.2 of OpenID Connect core" — capitalize and cite as OpenID Connect Core 1.0 [OIDC], consistent with the rest of the document.
items.title: [Editorial] Cite "OpenID Connect core" properly

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

In the Setup Phase, the numbered list of OP actions runs mid-sentence into unnumbered normative requirements on the **CP** ("The CP MUST show a dialogue...", "The dialogue MUST provide the link...", "The actual act of granting MUST involve active user interaction."). The CP-side MUSTs are easy to miss and are formally attached to an OP-actions list.

**Proposed fix**
- Split into "OP requirements" and "CP requirements" subsections with their own lists.
items.title: [Editorial] Setup Phase CP requirements buried inside the OP action list

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The Introduction's actor list and the Actors section duplicate each other with slightly different wording — keep the normative description in Actors and trim the Introduction.

In the relationship figure, every edge is labeled (grants / instructs / allows) except the OP–CP edge; label it (e.g. "fetches claims").
items.title: [Editorial] Duplicate actor descriptions; unlabeled OP–CP edge in figure

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

- "the Clams Provider's UserInfo endpoint" → "Claims Provider's" (Introduction).
- "This process will be repeated for as each Claims Providers as necessary" → "for each Claims Provider as necessary" (UserInfo Endpoint Request).
- "it is comprised by over 160 participating entities" → "it comprises" / "it is composed of" (Foreword).
- "This OP retrieves a downscoped access token" → "The OP retrieves" (Claims Collection).
- "for every RP requests" → "for every RP request" (Setup Phase).
- "Once the necessary claim sets were collected" → "have been collected" (Claims Delivery).
- Delivery Phase step list: the Introduction's outline has the OP responding to the RP as its own step; the Delivery Phase numbered list jumps from Claims Collection to Claims Verification — add the response step.
items.title: [Editorial] Typos and grammar fixes

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

Claims Verification uses "Aggregate Claim" and "Aggregated Claims" interchangeably; elsewhere "claim sets" / "signed claims set" appear uncapitalized although "Claim Set" is a defined term.

**Proposed fix**
- Pick one defined term for the RP-facing artifact and use the defined "Claim Set" capitalization consistently.
items.title: [Editorial] Inconsistent terminology: "Aggregate Claim" / "Aggregated Claims" / "Claim Set"

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The Abstract lists six methods including "an RP to ask for **verified claims** to the OP"; the Scope section lists five, dropping that one — the two lists should match.

Also, "verified claims" evokes OpenID Connect for Identity Assurance (`verified_claims`), which the draft never defines or references. Either cite OpenID4IDA or say "claims".
items.title: [Editorial] Abstract/Scope mismatch; "verified claims" undefined

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The -04 Document History entry says "Stated trust model", but no trust model section appears anywhere in the document. The intended content is presumably the model discussed in #1.

**Proposed fix**
- Add the trust model section (see #1), or correct the changelog.
items.title: [Editorial] Changelog claims "Stated trust model" but no trust model section exists

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

Claims Delivery says the OP creates the response per OIDC Core §5.6.2, but not **where** the aggregated claims appear — ID Token or OP UserInfo response (Core allows both) — nor how the OP signals partial failure: CP unreachable, CP token expired/revoked, consent withdrawn, claims no longer available.

**Proposed fix**
- Specify (or explicitly leave to the RP request syntax) whether aggregated claims are returned in the ID Token, UserInfo response, or both.
- Define behavior for partial results and an error signal RPs can rely on (e.g. omitted claim sources plus a defined error member).
items.title: [Interop] Delivery location and error semantics unspecified

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

OIDC Dynamic Client Registration defines `policy_uri`. Both the Setup Phase ("the link to the `policy_url` provided by the OP during its registration") and Subject Granting ("the link to the RP provided policy_url") say `policy_url`. Implementations following the letter of this draft will not interoperate.

**Proposed fix**
- s/policy_url/policy_uri/ in both places.
items.title: [Interop] policy_url is not the registered parameter name (should be policy_uri)

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

In the Discovery Phase (which is about **Claims Provider** metadata): "The following optional OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 parameters are now required in the **OpenID Provider Metadata**: `claim_types_supported`... MUST contain the value *aggregated*."

A CP returns *normal* claims to the OP; it is the **OP's** metadata (toward RPs) that should advertise `aggregated`. Note also that issue #1 proposes exactly that OP-side use (metadata statement of the trust provisions). As written, it is ambiguous which entity carries the requirement, and the draft is silently changing the optionality of an existing Discovery parameter.

**Proposed fix**
- Move/duplicate the requirement to an explicit "OP Metadata" section: the OP MUST publish `claim_types_supported` containing the value `aggregated` in its metadata.
- If any CP-side signal is needed, define it separately and explain why.
items.title: [Interop] claim_types_supported requirement targets the wrong (or ambiguous) entity

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

In Normative references:

- [JWT]/[JWS]/[JWE]/[JWA] cite `draft-ietf-*` URLs instead of RFC 7519 / 7515 / 7516 / 7518.
- RFC 7636 is invoked in "Terms and definitions" but absent from the reference list.
- The Notational Conventions text cites [RFC2119] [RFC8174], but only [BCP14] appears in the reference list.
- [OpenID.Registration] uses `http://`; the `tools.ietf.org` URLs should be `rfc-editor.org` or `datatracker.ietf.org`.
- RFC 9700 and RFC 9207 should be added per the security issues from this review.
items.title: [Interop] Reference rot: pre-RFC draft URLs for JWT/JWS/JWE/JWA; RFC 7636 missing; BCP 14 mismatch

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

Claims Collection's downscoping mechanism cites "section 12 of OpenID Connect 1.0" — that section is *Using Refresh Tokens*. But the Introduction says refresh tokens are optional in this specification. An implementation without refresh tokens has no defined downscoping path — and arguably no defined path to long-lived out-of-sync access at all: OIDC requires the `offline_access` scope (with `prompt=consent`) for tokens usable without the user present, which the Setup Phase never mentions.

**Proposed fix**
- Reconcile: either require the OP to obtain and use a refresh token when it performs downscoping or out-of-sync collection, or define an alternative (e.g. token exchange, RFC 8693).
- Require the OP to include `offline_access` (with `prompt=consent`) in the Setup Phase Authentication Request.
items.title: [Interop] Downscoping depends on refresh tokens that are optional; offline_access never mentioned

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The Discovery Phase defines `userinfo_signed_response_alg` as a CP **metadata** parameter holding a JSON array. Problems:

1. OIDC Discovery already defines `userinfo_signing_alg_values_supported` for exactly this purpose.
2. `userinfo_signed_response_alg` is the OIDC *client registration* parameter (a single string). Reusing that name in provider metadata with a different type and semantics guarantees confusion.
3. It is marked **Optional**, while signed UserInfo is a MUST for CPs — the OP cannot select an algorithm it cannot discover.

**Proposed fix**
- Require the CP to publish `userinfo_signing_alg_values_supported` in its metadata (Required, not Optional), and keep `userinfo_signed_response_alg` strictly as the client registration parameter.
items.title: [Interop] userinfo_signed_response_alg as CP metadata collides with the registration parameter and duplicates userinfo_signing_alg_values_supported

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The RP MUST verify CP signatures and check that the issuers are trusted (Claims Verification steps 1 and 3), but the draft never says how the RP resolves a CP `iss` to verification keys — CP Discovery `jwks_uri`? Pre-configuration? A trust framework / OpenID Federation?

Combined with the unspecified JWT content requirements (see the algorithm-confusion issue), the verification chapter is not implementable end-to-end.

**Proposed fix**
- Specify key resolution (e.g. RP resolves the embedded JWT's `iss` via OIDC Discovery to `jwks_uri`), and note trust-framework/Federation alternatives.
items.title: [Interop] Key discovery for RP verification of CP signatures is unspecified

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

Both the Delivery Phase intro and "Claims Request by RP to OP" say the RP "MUST use the OpenID Connect Authentication Request **with extension parameters defined in this document**" — but Draft 04 defines none (they were removed in -03 along with the claims endpoint). Likewise, "OP MUST implement mandatory to implement extensions that this document defines" (Actors → OP) points at nothing.

There is currently **no syntax** for an RP to request aggregated claims, name acceptable CPs/issuers, or request freshness. This is the core interop surface of the spec.

**Proposed fix**
- Define the request syntax (e.g. a `claims`-parameter extension naming requested claim sources/issuers), or explicitly state that the standard `claims`/`scope` parameters are used as-is and delete the dangling references.
items.title: [Interop] RP request "extension parameters defined in this document" are not defined

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

Claims Verification step 4 requires the RP to "verify that the *aud* (audience) Claim is that of the OP's Issuer Identifier". Per OIDC Core, a signed UserInfo response's `aud` is the **client_id the CP issued to the OP** — which, under the Dynamic Registration flow this draft mandates, is an opaque CP-chosen string, not the OP's issuer URL.

As written, conforming implementations will hard-fail on every response.

**Proposed fix — one of:**
- Add a CP requirement to set `aud` in the signed UserInfo JWT to the OP's Issuer Identifier (new CP behavior, currently absent from the CP section); or
- Change the RP verification rule to match what CPs actually emit, and define how the RP learns the OP's client_id at the CP (probably undesirable).
items.title: [Interop] RP aud verification cannot succeed under dynamic registration

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The Registration Phase says "the OP MUST NOT register `userinfo_encrypted_response_alg`", forbidding JWE protection of claim content beyond TLS. If the rationale is that the OP must forward the CP's JWS verbatim to RPs, a nested JWT (JWS inside a JWE decrypted by the OP) achieves that while adding confidentiality in transit and at CDNs/proxies.

As written, the draft bans a privacy control, lists JWE as a normative reference it never uses, and gives no rationale.

**Proposed fix**
- Either allow (and describe) nested JWS-in-JWE UserInfo responses, or state the rationale for the prohibition and drop the unused JWE reference.
items.title: [Privacy] Prohibiting userinfo_encrypted_response_alg bans a confidentiality control

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

At Setup, the Subject consents at the CP to disclosure to "potentially unspecified RPs" in the future. The per-RP consent dialogue at the OP is the compensating control — but that makes the CP-side consent contingent on OP honesty, which is not stated.

**Proposed fix**
- State the reliance explicitly in Privacy Considerations.
- Recommend that CPs provide users an interface to review and revoke standing OP grants.
items.title: [Privacy] Open-ended consent at Setup Phase relies on OP honesty

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The "sufficiently large" Setup Phase grant means the OP acquires — and MAY store — claims no RP has asked for, indefinitely. The only user control required is a UI to *view* stored claims; there is no requirement to let the Subject delete stored claim sets or revoke the OP's grant at the CP, and no retention guidance.

**Proposed fix**
- Require (or at least recommend) that the OP provide deletion of stored claim sets and a pointer to grant revocation at the CP.
- Add data-minimization and retention-limit guidance to Privacy Considerations (relevant for GDPR-style regimes).
items.title: [Privacy] Over-collection and unbounded retention; no deletion or revocation requirements

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

Privacy Considerations covers only RP–RP collusion via `sub`. Missing:

1. The CP's `sub` embedded in the signed JWT is pairwise **per OP**, so all RPs see the *same* CP `sub` and the same CP signature — enabling RP–RP *and* RP–CP correlation.
2. Signed claims are **non-repudiable**: an RP can cryptographically prove the user's attribute values to arbitrary third parties, which plaintext claims do not allow.

**Proposed fix**
- Extend Privacy Considerations to cover both, and discuss mitigations (ephemeral/per-delivery CP subject identifiers, per-RP re-issuance, selective disclosure formats such as SD-JWT).
items.title: [Privacy] Correlation analysis incomplete: RP–CP collusion, common CP sub across RPs, non-repudiation

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

In the aggregated model the OP sees the **content** of every claim from every CP, plus which RPs receive which claims, for every transaction. This is the fundamental privacy trade-off versus the distributed model (and versus wallet-style presentation), and the Privacy Considerations section — currently one sentence — does not mention it.

Conversely, a genuine privacy *benefit* worth stating: with out-of-sync collection, CPs do not learn which RPs the user visits or when (no phone-home).

**Proposed fix**
- Add Privacy Considerations text describing OP visibility/centralization, the no-phone-home property versus CPs, and guidance for deployments that need to limit OP visibility (e.g. future selective-disclosure mechanisms).
items.title: [Privacy] The OP as a full-visibility aggregation point is not discussed

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The Security Considerations section only incorporates OIDC Core and Dynamic Client Registration by reference. Given the new trust topology this document creates (OP as client to many CPs, long-lived broad grants, RP verification of third-party-signed JWTs), that is not sufficient.

**Proposed fix**
- Add RFC 9700 as a normative reference and profile its applicable requirements (mix-up, PKCE, sender-constraining, refresh token protection, redirect URI validation).
- Track [draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics-update](https://www.ietf.org/archive/id/draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics-update-03.html) (extension of BCP 240) and profile its attack classes, all of which apply to this topology: audience injection (#35), cross-toolkit account takeover / connection context binding (#36), cross-user session fixation (#37), and shared consent in brokered OAuth (#38). Reference it normatively once published as part of BCP 240.
- Fold in the specific analyses filed as separate issues from this review (mix-up, algorithm confusion, sub binding, claim-set replay, staleness, OP compromise).
items.title: [Security] Security Considerations is a single sentence; RFC 9700 should be a normative reference

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

Two related points missing from Security Considerations:

1. The CP-signed JWTs are audienced (at best) to the OP, not to any RP, and are handed to every RP by design. Any RP — or anyone who exfiltrates one — can forward a claim set elsewhere; acceptance depends entirely on the receiving party's verification discipline.
2. The OP accumulates long-lived CP tokens plus signed claim sets for its whole user base (RFC 9700 §4.10, misuse of stolen tokens, applies). This concentration of bearer credentials and non-repudiable personal data makes the OP a high-value target.

**Proposed fix**
- Discuss replay of embedded claim sets across RPs and mitigations (short lifetimes, per-delivery re-issuance where feasible).
- Add storage/protection requirements for the OP's token and claim-set stores.
items.title: [Security] Embedded claim sets are replayable bearer artifacts; OP token/claims store is a honeypot

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

"RP authentication and the request verification" says for unsigned requests the OP "MUST at least verify that the client_id is valid", omitting exact `redirect_uri` matching, which RFC 9700 §4.1 makes a MUST for authorization servers. The NOTE "RP MUST be authenticated at one point or another before completion of the transaction" is not implementable as written — public RPs cannot authenticate; presumably the intent is code-to-client binding via client authentication or PKCE at the token endpoint.

**Proposed fix**
- Require the OP to compare the `redirect_uri` against the pre-registered values using exact string matching.
- Replace the NOTE with a precise requirement: the OP MUST bind the authorization code to the RP's client_id, and the OP MUST redeem the code only upon client authentication (confidential clients) or presentation of a valid PKCE verifier (public clients).
items.title: [Security] RP request verification: no exact redirect_uri matching; vague RP authentication requirement (RFC 9700 §4.1)

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

"Claims Collection MAY be done out of sync", but there is no maximum age, no required `iat`/`exp` check by the RP, and no way for an RP to demand freshly collected claims. A user could revoke the OP's grant at the CP, or the underlying attribute could change, and the OP can keep serving old signed claim sets indefinitely.

**Proposed fix**
- Require the CP to include `iat`/`exp` in its signed JWTs, and require the RP to validate them.
- Define a way for the RP to express maximum acceptable claim age (analogous to `max_age`) and for the OP to trigger fresh collection.
- Discuss grant revocation at the CP and its (non-)effect on already-collected claim sets.
items.title: [Security] No freshness or revocation semantics for out-of-sync collected claim sets

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The `sub` inside the CP-signed JWT is the CP's (likely pairwise) identifier for the OP account; the RP has no way to verify it refers to the same person as the `sub` in the OP's ID Token. The RP relies entirely on OP honesty — a compromised or malicious OP can substitute another user's claim set undetectably.

This is the security-considerations side of the trust model discussed in #1: if the ecosystem model is "the OP is trusted to bind CP tokens to the correct account" (provisions 1–3 in #1), the specification needs to state that assumption and its failure mode (cross-user claim injection by a compromised OP) explicitly in the Security Considerations, so that trust frameworks can decide whether/how to audit it.

**Proposed fix**
- Adopt the trust-model text from #1 into the spec body.
- Add a Security Considerations entry describing the residual risk when the OP is compromised.
items.title: [Security] Nothing binds the embedded claim set to the authenticated subject (cross-user claim injection)

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

Claims Verification step 1 says the RP verifies the signature "using the algorithm specified in the JWT *alg* Header Parameter". Having the verifier take the algorithm from the attacker-controllable header is the classic JWS algorithm-confusion pitfall. `alg: none` is excluded only in the Discovery metadata description, not in the RP verification rules.

**Proposed fix**
- Require the RP to validate the `alg` against an expected/allowlisted set (e.g. what the CP advertises in `userinfo_signing_alg_values_supported`) before verification.
- Require the RP to reject `alg: none` and unsecured JWTs, stated in the verification rules themselves.
- Require the CP to include `iss`, `sub`, `aud`, `iat`, and `exp` in the signed JWT, so that the RP can implement the other verification MUSTs.
items.title: [Security] Claims Verification: signature algorithm taken from attacker-controllable JWT header

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The Setup Phase says the grant "SHOULD be sufficiently large so that it will reduce the number of times that OP needs to take the Subject to the CP". Deliberately over-scoping is the opposite of RFC 9700 §2.3 (access token privilege restriction). The downscoping SHOULD in Claims Collection limits what the CP *returns* per request, but the OP still *holds* an over-privileged long-lived credential.

This is a deliberate design trade-off (fewer consent round-trips), but it needs to be acknowledged and compensated.

**Proposed fix**
- Acknowledge the trade-off in Security Considerations.
- Add compensating controls: require the OP to safeguard stored tokens; recommend that the CP issue short-lived access tokens, support token revocation (RFC 7009), and audience-restrict the access tokens it issues to its own UserInfo endpoint.
items.title: [Security] "Sufficiently large" grant contradicts least-privilege guidance (RFC 9700 §2.3)

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The Setup Phase instructs that the grant "SHOULD be sufficiently large" and the resulting access/refresh tokens are held long-term for out-of-sync claims collection. Draft -02 required MTLS or DPoP sender-constraining; -03 rolled that back with no replacement and no rationale. The result is a store of high-value, broad-scope **bearer** tokens at the OP.

RFC 9700 §4.14 requires refresh tokens for public clients to be sender-constrained or rotated, and §2.2 recommends sender-constraining (MTLS [RFC 8705] / DPoP [RFC 9449]) generally.

**Proposed fix**
- Recommend that the CP sender-constrain the access and refresh tokens it issues to the OP (RFC 8705 or RFC 9449).
- Require the CP to either rotate refresh tokens or sender-constrain them.
- Recommend that the OP authenticate to the CP's token endpoint with an asymmetric client authentication method (e.g. `private_key_jwt`), per RFC 9700 §2.5. Note: because the OP authenticates to multiple CPs, the OP MUST then also apply the audience-injection countermeasures of draft-ietf-oauth-security-topics-update §2.1 — see #35.
items.title: [Security] Long-lived broad-scope bearer tokens: no sender-constraining, no refresh token rotation (RFC 9700 §2.2, §4.14)

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The Setup Phase only says "the OP MUST use an OpenID Connect Authentication Request" — it does not pin `response_type`, and it imposes no PKCE, `state`, or `nonce` requirements.

Per RFC 9700 §2.1.1, public clients MUST use PKCE and confidential clients SHOULD use PKCE (or, for OIDC clients, may rely on `nonce`), to prevent authorization code injection (§4.5) and CSRF (§4.7). The implicit grant is also not prohibited, contrary to RFC 9700 §2.1.2. Note that RFC 7636 is invoked in "Terms and definitions" but never used normatively.

**Proposed fix**
- Require the OP to send `response_type=code` in the Setup Phase Authentication Request.
- Require the OP to use PKCE (S256) or `nonce`, and to validate `state` and the `iss` response parameter, per RFC 9700.
- Prohibit the OP from using the implicit or hybrid flows to receive tokens from CPs in the front channel.
items.title: [Security] Setup Phase lacks PKCE/state/nonce and response_type requirements (RFC 9700 §2.1.1, §4.5, §4.7)

items.body:
_From a security/privacy/interoperability/consistency review of **openid-connect-claims-aggregation-1_0, Draft 04**, checked against its normative references and [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700.html) (OAuth 2.0 Security BCP)._

The OP acts as an OAuth/OIDC client to **multiple** CPs (Setup Phase). This is exactly the multi-AS topology targeted by mix-up attacks: a compromised or malicious CP can confuse the OP into sending an authorization code or access token belonging to an honest CP to the attacker.

RFC 9700 §4.4 requires clients that interact with multiple authorization servers to use the `iss` authorization response parameter ([RFC 9207](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9207.html)) or, alternatively, distinct per-issuer redirect URIs. Draft 04 says nothing about this.

**Proposed fix**
- Setup Phase: require the OP to validate the `iss` authorization response parameter (RFC 9207) or use per-CP redirect URIs.
- Discovery Phase: require/recommend CPs to publish `authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported`.
- Add RFC 9207 and RFC 9700 as normative references.
items.title: [Security] No mix-up attack defense for the OP-to-CP flows (RFC 9700 §4.4)

items.body:
## Summary

The SSF 1.0 specification defines two SSF-specific event types:

* `https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/ssf/event-type/verification`
* `https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/ssf/event-type/stream-updated`

Both event type URIs use the common prefix:

```text
https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/ssf/event-type/
```

However, SSF does not explicitly declare this prefix as the base URI for SSF event types.

## Background

The related CAEP and RISC event profile specifications explicitly declare the base URI used for their event types.

For example, [CAEP 1.0 Section 3](https://openid.net/specs/openid-caep-1_0-final.html#section-3) states:

> The base URI for CAEP event types is:
>
> `https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/caep/event-type/`

[RISC 1.0 Section 2](https://openid.net/specs/openid-risc-1_0-final.html#section-2) similarly declares:

> The base URI for RISC event types is:
>
> `https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/risc/event-type/`

SCIM Events also defines a common event URN namespace in [RFC 9967 Section 7.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9967.html#section-7.3-3.4.1).

SSF already follows the same general naming convention for its stream-related event types, but the common base URI is currently only implicit.

## Proposal

Add an explicit declaration to the SSF specification, close to the definitions of the SSF-specific event types.

Suggested text:

> The base URI for SSF event types is:
>
> `https://schemas.openid.net/secevent/ssf/event-type/`

Optionally, SSF could introduce a dedicated subsection for SSF event types and list the currently defined event types:

* `verification`
* `stream-updated`

## Rationale

This change would:

* document the common namespace already used by SSF-defined events;
* align SSF with the conventions used by CAEP and RISC;
* make the namespace easier for implementers to discover;
* provide a clearly defined namespace for potential future SSF-level events;
* avoid requiring readers to infer the base URI from individual event type definitions.

This would be an editorial clarification only. It would not change any existing event type URI or protocol behavior.
items.title: Explicitly declare the base URI for SSF event types

items.body:
OID4VP should clarify how OAuth extension specifications influence the requirements for authorization request parameters.

For example, an OAuth Authorization Request normally requires the `response_type` parameter. However, when using JWT Secured Authorization Requests (JAR), JAR states that the parameters contained in the Request Object are authoritative, meaning that parameters outside the Request Object are ignored for processing. Also note that as per JAR, `response_type` is optional and no longer mandatory in the initial request.

Without an explicit statement, this can create ambiguity as to whether parameters such as `response_type` are always required at the HTTP request level, or whether the requirements defined by OAuth extension specifications (such as JAR) take precedence.

Proposal:

Add a general statement that OAuth parameters defined outside of this specification must be used according to the applicable OAuth core and extension specifications.

This would make it clear that, for example, when JAR is used, the rules defined by JAR regarding Request Object processing take precedence over the generic OAuth Authorization Request parameter requirements, avoiding ambiguities around parameters such as `response_type`.
items.title: Clarify how OAuth extension specifications affect authorization request parameter requirements

Section 4.3 currently states:

> Wallets MUST authenticate themselves at the PAR endpoint using the same rules as defined in Section 4.4 for client authentication at the token endpoint.

However, Section 4.4 does not define any rules for client authentication at the token endpoint, so the reference is currently incorrect.

In practice, because HAIP requires FAPI, client authentication at the PAR endpoint is mandatory through the referenced FAPI requirements. Nevertheless, the current wording is confusing because it points to a section that does not actually define the referenced behavior.

Proposal:

Update the text in Section 4.3 to reference the appropriate normative source for client authentication, rather than Section 4.4, or alternatively add the missing client authentication rules to Section 4.4 if that was the original intent.

This would make the specification internally consistent while preserving the existing interoperability requirements.

items.body:
The specification uses the terms **terminate**, **reject**, and **return an error** in different contexts. Clarification is requested on the expected behavior and distinction between these terms.

### 1. `terminate`

Reference: [[OpenID4VP Section 5.10.1](https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-presentations-1_0.html#section-5.10.1-5)](https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-presentations-1_0.html#section-5.10.1-5)

> The Wallet MUST extract the set of Authorization Request parameters from the Request Object. The Wallet MUST only use the parameters in this Request Object, even if the same parameter was provided in an Authorization Request query parameter. The Client Identifier value in the client_id Authorization Request parameter and the Request Object client_id claim value MUST be identical, including the Client Identifier Prefix. If any of these conditions are not met, the Wallet MUST terminate request processing.

Our understanding is that **terminate** represents a hard stop in request processing. In this case, the Wallet does not continue the VP flow and does not notify the Verifier.

### 2. `reject`

Reference: [[OpenID4VP Section 5.8](https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-presentations-1_0.html#section-5-8)](https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-presentations-1_0.html#section-5-8)

> The Wallet MUST ignore any unrecognized parameters, other than the transaction_data parameter. One exception to this rule is the transaction_data parameter. Wallets that do not support this parameter MUST reject requests that contain it.

### 3. `return an error`

Reference: [[OpenID4VP Section 8.4](https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-presentations-1_0.html#section-8.4-3)](https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-presentations-1_0.html#section-8.4-3)

> If the Wallet does not support transaction_data parameter, it MUST return an error upon receiving a request that includes it.

## Clarification Required

For `terminate`, the expected behavior appears clear: the Wallet stops processing immediately without notifying the Verifier.

However, there is ambiguity regarding the difference between **reject** and **return an error**.

Specifically, for a Wallet that does not support the `transaction_data` parameter:

* Does **reject** mean that the Wallet should stop processing the request locally without notifying the Verifier, or should the Wallet notify the Verifier before ending the VP flow?
* Does **return an error** mean that the Wallet should notify the Verifier through the available error reporting mechanism before ending the VP flow?

For example, if the VP request contains `transaction_data` and uses `direct_post` response mode with a `response_uri`, should the Wallet notify to Verifier:

```http
POST /response_uri

{
  "error": "invalid_transaction_data",
  "error_description": "Transaction data feature is not supported by the Wallet"
}
```


Could you please clarify:

1. The intended distinction between **terminate**, **reject**, and **return an error**.
2. Whether **reject** and **return an error** result in different Wallet behaviors.
items.title: Clarification Request: Interpretation of terminate, reject, and return an error in OpenID4VP

## Description

Requesting clarification on whether the `request_uri` response can be an unsigned JWS or if it is required to be signed.

## Use Case

For clients using the `redirect_uri` prefix, signed requests are not supported. In this scenario, is reference mode using `request_uri` achievable with an unsigned `request_uri` response?

Example JWT header:

```json
{
  "alg": "none"
}
```

Example JWS:

```
eyJhbGciOiJub25lIn0./*Payload in B64 encoded form*/.
```

## References

The following references indicate that the `request_uri` response is expected to be signed:

**OpenID4VP — Request URI Response**

> The Request URI response MUST be an HTTP response with the content type `application/oauth-authz-req+jwt` and the body being a signed, optionally encrypted ([[OpenID4VP ref](https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-presentations-1_0.html#section-5.10.1-1)](https://openid.net/specs/openid-4-verifiable-presentations-1_0.html#section-5.10.1-1)).

**RFC 9101 — Authorization Request Object**

> The Authorization Request Object MUST be one of the following:
> (a) JWS signed
> (b) JWS signed and JWE encrypted
> ([[RFC 9101 ref](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9101/#section-5-7)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9101/#section-5-7))

Based on these requirements, clarification is requested on whether an unsigned `request_uri` response is permitted or if signing is mandatory.
items.title: Clarification on Request URI response

items.body:
**Context.** We implemented OpenID4VP 1.0 `transaction_data` end-to-end for a research prototype (per-action, human-in-the-loop authorization of a delegated action): an SD-JWT VC credential, a `payment`-style `transaction_data` entry, presented from the EUDI reference wallet (a commit-pinned research build) to a conformant verifier. It works end-to-end — request accepted, per-action user confirmation, and the verifier returns 200 once `transaction_data_hashes` is bound into the holder KB-JWT. Sharing two small things back to the WG. (This is a spec-side note to the DCP WG; distinct from the EUDI wallet-app implementation gap we filed separately at eu-digital-identity-wallet/eudi-app-android-wallet-ui#636.)

## 1. A worked KB-JWT example the spec could carry (non-normative)

The single most useful missing artefact when building this was one concrete, end-to-end example that walks from the `transaction_data` array value, through the hash, into the holder KB-JWT. A conformant verifier rejected our first attempts until the KB-JWT carried both `transaction_data_hashes` and `transaction_data_hashes_alg: sha-256` (verifier error: `'transaction_data_hashes_alg' must be 'sha-256'`). Once bound, the same verifier accepted.

A fully worked example — the hash below is real and recomputable:

Transaction Data object (before encoding):

```json
{"type":"payment","credential_ids":["payment_card"],"transaction_data_hashes_alg":["sha-256"],"payee":"ACME GmbH","amount":"120.00","currency":"EUR"}
```

Value as it appears in the `transaction_data` array (base64url, no padding):

```
eyJ0eXBlIjoicGF5bWVudCIsImNyZWRlbnRpYWxfaWRzIjpbInBheW1lbnRfY2FyZCJdLCJ0cmFuc2FjdGlvbl9kYXRhX2hhc2hlc19hbGciOlsic2hhLTI1NiJdLCJwYXllZSI6IkFDTUUgR21iSCIsImFtb3VudCI6IjEyMC4wMCIsImN1cnJlbmN5IjoiRVVSIn0
```

Hash entry = `base64url( SHA-256( the base64url string above ) )`, no padding (cf. #418):

```
Xzo6puFg3O2W4vzj3HgQKEROrFEEa8lwkQHFAkM5ff8
```

Holder KB-JWT payload (SD-JWT VC presentation), hash bound in:

```json
{
  "nonce": "<verifier-nonce>",
  "aud": "x509_hash:<verifier-cert-thumbprint>",
  "iat": "<unix-time>",
  "sd_hash": "<hash-of-issued-sd-jwt>",
  "transaction_data_hashes": ["Xzo6puFg3O2W4vzj3HgQKEROrFEEa8lwkQHFAkM5ff8"],
  "transaction_data_hashes_alg": "sha-256"
}
```

Reviewer self-check (reproduces the hash entry):

```
printf %s '<the base64url string>' | openssl dgst -sha256 -binary | basenc --base64url | tr -d '='
```

If a short non-normative worked example like this would be welcome in the Transaction Data section, I'm happy to open a PR — implementers seem to hit the same "which JWT, which claims, what is the hash input" questions we did.

## 2. One binding detail to confirm — multi-credential `credential_ids`

For a single presented credential the binding is unambiguous. For a presentation of **multiple** credentials where different `transaction_data` entries carry different `credential_ids`, we read the spec as: each presented credential's KB-JWT should carry hashes for **only** those `transaction_data` objects whose `credential_ids` reference that credential (per-credential filtering), not the full set. Is that the intended behaviour? We could not find a reference implementation exercising the multi-credential case to check against, so we'd like to confirm the reading before contributing test vectors for it.

## Offer

We have a working wallet + verifier setup and can contribute (a) the non-normative KB-JWT example above and (b) interop test vectors for both the single- and multi-credential `transaction_data` cases, if useful.

Thanks — glad to be contributing.

— Anton Sokolov, Tyche Institute (Tallinn); contribution agreements signed with the OpenID Foundation.
items.title: transaction_data: interop report + offer of a worked KB-JWT example (multi-credential credential_ids binding)

items.body:
A question / a need for clarification on the trust mark status endpoint response that arise from comments from @hmffa:

The description of the Trust Mark Status Reponse states:

> A **successful** response MUST use the HTTP status code 200 with the content type application/trust-mark-status-response+jwt, containing a signed JWT that is a Trust Mark Status Response.

The `status` claim contains descriptions for different status (positive and negative), among them:

> invalid: Signature validation failed or another error was detected

And at the end of the section:

>  If the Trust Mark Issuer receives a request about the status of an unknown Trust Mark, something it did not issue or is not aware of, it MUST respond with an HTTP status code 404 (Not found).

This is a bit confusing and potentially inconsistent / contradicting:
- It is not entirely clear when a response is "successful" and when it is an error response. Since a successful response can also contain error cases.
- Also the last sentence states that if the endpoint receives something that was not issued by the issuer it should return a 404 not found status code. But the description on the `status` claim says signature validation errors result in a response with `status=invalid`. 
Now from this different weird cases could arise:

| Was Issued By Issuer | Signature Valid | Comment | Response | 
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Yes | Yes | Everything fine | status=active|
| Yes | No | | status=invalid |
| No | Yes | !!! Someone else could create a correct signature !!! | 404 |
| No | No | What to do? | 404? status=invalid |

Is the 404 response actually needed? I don't see a case where the endpoint would receive a a trust mark for an "unknown Trust Mark, something it did not issue or is not aware of" that would not also have an invalid signature.

I believe that the last sentence with the 404 not found response is a left-over from the time where this endpoint did not receive a trust mark jwt but a trust mark type.
items.title: TM status response edge cases

Somewhat related to #8

We need an agreement on and common description of what data should be signed over by the device and what protection guarantees we need.

Historically in OpenID4VP, there was a bit of divergence, where the data being signed over by the Wallet was slightly different between the formats. We should align on a generic definition what exactly we sign over and how that is constructed. SessionTranscript is reconstructed, whereas KB-JWT contained the values and both contain different values (e.g., JwkTumbprint)

SessionTranscript for mDoc (vanilla OpenID4VP):

> OpenID4VPHandover = [
>   "OpenID4VPHandover", ; A fixed identifier for this handover type
>   OpenID4VPHandoverInfoHash ; A cryptographic hash of OpenID4VPHandoverInfo
> ]
> 
> ; Contains the sha-256 hash of OpenID4VPHandoverInfoBytes
> OpenID4VPHandoverInfoHash = bstr
> 
> ; Contains the bytes of OpenID4VPHandoverInfo encoded as CBOR
> OpenID4VPHandoverInfoBytes = bstr .cbor OpenID4VPHandoverInfo
> 
> OpenID4VPHandoverInfo = [
>   clientId,
>   nonce,

>   responseUri
> ] ; Array containing handover parameters
> 
> clientId = tstr
> 
> nonce = tstr
> 
> jwkThumbprint = bstr
> 
> responseUri = tstr

This is kb-jwt for SD-JWT VC (vanilla OpenID4VP)

There has been some prior discussion in the different WGs on advanced query language features with the main historic discussion point being value matching: Value matching as defined in OpenID4VP (see https://openid.github.io/OpenID4VP/openid-4-verifiable-presentations-1_0-wg-draft.html#selecting_claims) allows a Verifier to request a specific claim and provide a hint on the expected value.

There has been some discussions around what exactly should be normatively said around value matching and how to best make it work for different wallet architectures etc. while preventing all potential leakage of information.

Current text in OpenID4VP on value matching:

> When a Claims Query contains a restriction on the values of a claim, the Wallet SHOULD NOT return the claim if its value does not match according to the rules for values defined in [Section 6.3](https://openid.github.io/OpenID4VP/openid-4-verifiable-presentations-1_0-wg-draft.html#claims_query), i.e., the claim should be treated the same as if it did not exist in the Credential. Implementing this restriction may not be possible in all cases, for example, if the Wallet does not have access to the claim value before presentation or user consent or if another component routing the request to the Wallet does not have access to the claim value. It is ultimately up to the Wallet and/or the End-User if the value matching request is followed. Therefore, Verifiers MUST treat restrictions expressed using values as a best-effort way to improve user privacy, but MUST NOT rely on it for security checks.

with these privacy considerations:

> When using DCQL values to match the expected values of claims, the fact that a claim within a certain Credential matched a value or did not match a value might already leak information about the claim value. Therefore, Wallets MUST take precautions against leaking information about the claim value when processing values. This SHOULD include, in particular:
> 
> - ensuring that a Verifier, in the response, cannot distinguish between the case where an End-User did not consent to releasing the Credential and the case where the claim value did not match the expected value, and
> - preventing repeated or "silent" requests leaking data to the Verifier without the user's consent by ensuring that all requests, even if no response can be sent by the Wallet due to a values mismatch, require some form of End-User interaction before a response is sent.
>
>In both cases listed here, it needs to be considered that returning an error response can also leak information about the processing outcome of values.

More generally speaking, there have also been discussions on more advanced syntax in the query language with one such example being value in array (e.g., specific country in nationalities array)
items.title: Query Language: Value Matching

> *Originally submitted by **josephheenan** (Joseph Heenan) on 2026-03-16*


The last published working group draft of FAPI-CIBA was in 2019 (what became the first implementer's draft).

> *Originally submitted by **Nat** (Nat Sakimura) on 2025-09-17*


In the Sept 17 call, in AOB, AP2 Imapcs to FAPI was talked about. We decided to track it as a task.

Following is the copy of my email to the list that kicked off this discussion.

---

I came across the news that Google announced ["Powering AI commerce with the new Agent Payments Protocol \(AP2\)" ](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/announcing-agents-to-payments-ap2-protocol?hl=en)my morning today \(i.e. like 14 hours ago\). 

I have not grasped the protocol yet, but it is based on the A2A protocol and uses OAuth. Specifically, the "Sample Credential Provider Agent Card" code snippet within the technical implementation section of [AP2 Specification \[3\]](https://ap2-protocol.org/specification/) shows OAuth2 as part of its security configuration. This seems to indicate that a Credential Provider \(CP\) uses an OAuth2  for skills such as get\_payment\_methods, which retrieves a user's payment methods.

The configuration includes details for the authorizationCode flow, specifying an authorizationUrl, scopes \(particularly for `get_payment_methods`\), and a `tokenUrl`. This seems to indicate that OAuth2 is used by Credential Providers within the AP2 ecosystem to secure access to users' payment credentials

Intuit, Mastercard, Okta and PingIdentity seem to be contributing to it. 

**10 Key Points of Agent Payments Protocol \(AP2\)**

1. **Launch and Purpose**: AP2 is an **open protocol launched by Google on September 16, 2025**, developed with over 60 leading payments and technology companies. Its purpose is to **securely initiate and transact agent-led payments across platforms**.
2. **Extension of Existing Protocols**: It functions as an **extension of the Agent2Agent \(A2A\) protocol and Model Context Protocol \(MCP\)**.
3. **Payment-Agnostic Framework**: AP2 establishes a **payment-agnostic framework**, enabling secure transactions across all payment methods, including credit/debit cards, stablecoins, and real-time bank transfers.
4. **Addressing AI Agent Payment Challenges**: It addresses critical questions arising from AI agents transacting on behalf of users, such as **authorization, authenticity, and accountability**, which challenge traditional payment system assumptions.
5. **Trust through Mandates**: AP2 builds trust using **Mandates**—tamper-proof, cryptographically-signed digital contracts that serve as verifiable proof of user instructions. These are signed by **verifiable credentials \(VCs\).**
6. **Two User Scenarios**: Mandates support two primary user interaction scenarios:

◦ **Real-time Purchases \(human present\)**: An "Intent Mandate" is captured, and user approval signs a "Cart Mandate" for specific items and prices.

◦ **Delegated Tasks \(human not present\)**: A detailed "Intent Mandate" is signed upfront with rules, allowing the agent to automatically generate a "Cart Mandate" when conditions are met.

7. **Non-Repudiable Audit Trail**: The complete sequence from intent to cart to payment creates a **non-repudiable audit trail**, providing a clear foundation for accountability by answering questions of authorization and authenticity.
8. **Enabling New Commerce Experiences**: AP2's flexible design supports new commercial models like **smarter shopping, personalized offers, coordinated tasks, and B2B applications** for autonomous procurement.
9. **Support for Emerging Payment Systems**: It is designed as a universal protocol for **stablecoins and cryptocurrencies**, with Google collaborating with Coinbase and others to launch the **A2A x402 extension** for agent-based crypto payments.

10\. **Open Collaboration and Evolution**: Google is committed to evolving AP2 through an **open, collaborative process**, including engagement with standards bodies, and invites the entire payments and technology community to contribute via its public GitHub repository

**References**

1. Google Blog: Powering AI commerce with the new Agent Payments Protocol \(AP2\) [https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/announcing-agents-to-payments-ap2-protocol?hl=en](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/announcing-agents-to-payments-ap2-protocol?hl=en)
2. Agent Payments Protocol \(AP2\): [https://github.com/google-agentic-commerce/AP2](https://github.com/google-agentic-commerce/AP2)
3. AP2 Specification: [https://ap2-protocol.org/specification/#71-illustrative-transaction-flow](https://ap2-protocol.org/specification/#71-illustrative-transaction-flow)
4. A2A x402 Extension: [https://github.com/google-agentic-commerce/a2a-x402](https://github.com/google-agentic-commerce/a2a-x402)

Best, 

‌

Nat Sakimura

‌

> *Originally submitted by **Dima Postnikov** (Dima Postnikov) on 2025-08-06*


Current text says:

> Clients implementing FAPI2 authorization request signing:
>
> …
>
> shall send a `nbf` claim in the request object
>
> …

I understand that there are circumstances where it’s useful to have but is it required for every request?

Side question. Should this text from FAPI 2 security profile be in FAPI 2 message signing instead? 

> 1. to accommodate clock offsets, shall accept JWTs with an `iat` or `nbf` timestamp between 0 and 10 seconds in the future but shall reject JWTs with an `iat` or `nbf` timestamp greater than 60 seconds in the future. See Note 3 for further details and rationale; and
> 
> **NOTE 3**: Clock skew is a cause of many interoperability issues. Even a few hundred milliseconds of clock skew can cause JWTs to be rejected for being "issued in the future". The DPoP specification \[[RFC9449](https://openid.net/specs/fapi-security-profile-2_0-final.html#RFC9449)\] suggests that JWTs are accepted in the reasonably near future \(on the order of seconds or minutes\). This document goes further by requiring authorization servers to accept JWTs that have timestamps up to 10 seconds in the future. 10 seconds was chosen as a value that does not affect security while greatly increasing interoperability. Implementers are free to accept JWTs with a timestamp of up to 60 seconds in the future. Some ecosystems have found that the value of 30 seconds is needed to fully eliminate clock skew issues. To prevent implementations switching off `iat` and `nbf` checks completely this document imposes a maximum timestamp in the future of 60 seconds.
>
> ‌

‌

At some point we need to communicate the FAPI WG thoughts on post-quantum.

A quick set of thoughts:

1. TLS 1.3 \(or later\) will be required for post-quantum so we probably want to add a recommendation around moving off TLS 1.2 at some point

> *Originally submitted by **Takahiko Kawasaki** (Takahiko Kawasaki) on 2025-05-09*


Are there any standards other than OpenID Federation that allow resource servers to retrieve a client’s public key? To verify an HTTP message signature in a resource request, the resource server needs the client application’s public key - that is, the counterpart to the private key used to sign the HTTP message. However, there is currently no standardized way for the resource server to obtain this public key. Has there been any discussion in the community about standardizing a method for retrieving clients' public keys?

As far as I know, OpenID Federation is currently the only standard that enables resource servers to retrieve client metadata \(and subsequently the client’s public key via the `jwks_uri` property\). However, adopting OpenID Federation is too heavy for most API systems, as it requires authorized third parties to operate trust anchors and intermediate authorities.

A straightforward solution to obtain the client’s public key might be to include a property - such as `client_jwks_uri` - in the introspection response that indicates the location of the client’s JWK Set. But I’m not sure if that’s an appropriate approach…

---

items.body:
> *Originally submitted by **Takahiko Kawasaki** (Takahiko Kawasaki) on 2024-10-07*


There are two topics: one is how to identify the algorithm of a given HTTP message signature, and the other is whether to impose restrictions on the algorithms.

### How to identify the algorithm

Even if a key can be identified in a vendor-neutral manner by using the `keyid` parameter \([ISSUE 721](https://bitbucket.org/openid/fapi/issues/721)\), the verifier must be able to determine the algorithm for verification. Since JWTs always include the `alg` parameter \([RFC 7518 Section 3.1](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7518.html#section-3.1)\), identifying the algorithm is straightforward. However, HTTP message signatures do not always provide information about the algorithm.

The `alg` parameter \([RFC 9421 Section 2.3](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html#section-2.3)\) in the signature metadata appears to be usable, but [Section 3.3.7. JSON Web Signature \(JWS\) Algorithm](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html#section-3.3.7) of RFC 9421 explicitly states the following:

> JSON Web Algorithm \(JWA\) values from the "JSON Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms" registry are not included as signature parameters. Typically, the JWS algorithm can be signaled using JSON Web Keys \(JWKs\) or other mechanisms common to JOSE implementations. In fact, JWA values are not registered in the ["HTTP Signature Algorithms" registry](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html#hsa-registry) \([Section 6.2](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html#hsa-registry)\), and so **the explicit** `alg` **signature parameter is not used at all when using JOSE signing algorithms.**

This excerpted paragraph above implies that, when the key is represented as a JWK,  the `alg` parameter \([RFC 7517 Section 4.4](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7517.html#section-4.4)\) within the JWK should be referenced. However, the parameter is optional. Therefore, in practice, it is necessary to require the `alg` parameter within the JWK to be mandatory when the key is represented as a JWK. It may be worth mentioning this in the FAPI 2.0 Message Signing specification. Otherwise, client applications may register their public keys in JWK format without the `alg` parameter, leading to failed verification of HTTP message signatures. As a result, resource server providers will have to spend time instructing client application developers to include the `alg` parameter when registering JWKs.

### Whether to impose restrictons on the algorithm

It should be explicitly stated that the algorithms for HTTP message signatures are restricted to those listed in [Section 5.4. Cryptography and Secrets](https://openid.net/specs/fapi-2_0-security-profile.html#section-5.4) of the [FAPI 2.0 Security Profile](https://openid.net/specs/fapi-2_0-security-profile.html), if we intend to apply the same restrictions to them.

This is a minor detail, but the FAPI 2.0 Security Profile states _“when creating or processing JWTs.”_ However, the format of HTTP message signatures is not JWT. Therefore, unless explicitly required, the algorithm restrictions stated in the FAPI 2.0 Security Profile do not apply to HTTP message signatures.

Of course, it is also possible to decide not to impose such restrictions on the signature algorithms for HTTP message signatures.

‌

‌

‌

---
*Bitbucket status: **open*** 

*Bitbucket origin: [issue 722](https://bitbucket.org/openid/fapi/issues/722/algorithms-for-http-message-signatures)*
items.title: Algorithms for HTTP message signatures

items.body:
> *Originally submitted by **Takahiko Kawasaki** (Takahiko Kawasaki) on 2024-10-07*


It seems preferable to recommend including the `keyid` parameter \([RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html), [Section 2.3. Signature Parameters](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html#section-2.3)\) to the signature metadata of HTTP message signatures.

When used with the mandatory `created` and `tag` parameters, the `keyid` parameter will appear in the `Signature-Input` HTTP field as shown below.

```
GET /api/userinfo HTTP/1.1
Host: trial.authlete.net
User-Agent: curl/8.7.1
Accept: */*
Authorization: Bearer 4rSgHO6sdlBL4z_1l4bAmED2CG40zblXlc3YDqrqdu8
Signature-Input: sig=("method" "target-uri" "authorization")\
 ;created=1728051074\
 ;keyid="ScIdKFzAj93vywpwjrfi3wrj5oHmHbHfmPT5IPTLmVc"\
 ;tag="fapi-2-request"
Signature: sig=:yx+SthCcbAu7R7rV1DoZX8ILLURmHwNTlRXMbnJVRHWXwyHQQPmPnLLhNx9tHeqG8Mp1SeN4CSB38QDwKfkkqA==:
```

The reason for recommending the use of `keyid` is that it is the only vendor-neutral means for key identification.

Without the `keyid` parameter, the resource server’s implementation would have to identify the key based on its own custom rules, significantly reducing interoperability. As a result, fintech client applications would need to agree on different key identification methods for each finantial institution they communicate with. Additionally, without the `keyid` parameter, while not impossible, it would become considerably difficult to support the use case mentioned in the first paragraph of RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures, [Section 4.3. Multiple Signatures](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html#section-4.3), where _“a signer may include multiple signatures signing the same message components **with different keys** or algorithms to support verifiers with different capabilities.”_

‌

> *Originally submitted by **Takahiko Kawasaki** (Takahiko Kawasaki) on 2024-09-30*


It may be worth considering defining new error codes for HTTP message signature verification errors.

[RFC 9449 OAuth 2.0 Demonstrating Proof of Possession \(DPoP\)](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9449.html) has defined `invalid_dpop_proof` and `use_dpop_nonce` error codes for DPoP-related errors. Similarly, OAuth-aware applications using HTTP Message Signatures may want dedicated error codes for HTTP Message Signatures-related errors. For example, `invalid_http_message_signature`.

Without such dedicated error codes, the userinfo endpoint implementation I’m working on will eventually return `invalid_request` for HTTP message signature verification errors, as there doesn’t seem to be any more appropriate error code among the currently available ones.

items.body:
> *Originally submitted by **Takahiko Kawasaki** (Takahiko Kawasaki) on 2024-09-20*


[FAPI 2.0 Message Signing](https://openid.bitbucket.io/fapi/fapi-2_0-message-signing.html), [Section 5.6.2.1. Resource servers](https://openid.bitbucket.io/fapi/fapi-2_0-message-signing.html#section-5.6.2.1), the third clause says as follows:

> if the request was signed, shall include the request signature and request signature input in the response signature input by means of the `req` boolean flag defined in Section 2.4 of \[[RFC9421](https://openid.bitbucket.io/fapi/fapi-2_0-message-signing.html#RFC9421)\];

If this clause means that `"signature";req` and `"signature-input";req` must be included in the signature base \(and there seems to be no other way to interpret it\), then this clause should be removed.

The third-to-last paragraph of [Section 2.4. Signing Request Components in a Response Message](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html#section-2.4) in [RFC 9421 HTTP Message Signatures](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html) states the following and explicitly says it is “NOT RECOMMENDED” to do so for security reasons.

> While it is syntactically possible to include the Signature and Signature-Input fields of the request message in the signature components of a response to a message using this mechanism, this practice is **NOT RECOMMENDED**. This is because signatures of signatures do not provide transitive coverage of covered components as one might expect, and the practice is susceptible to several attacks as discussed in [Section 7.3.7](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9421.html#security-sign-signature). An application that needs to signal successful processing or receipt of a signature would need to carefully specify alternative mechanisms for sending such a signal securely.

‌

---

> *Originally submitted by **Takahiko Kawasaki** (Takahiko Kawasaki) on 2024-09-11*


An HTTP message can contain multiple HTTP message signatures. Does Section 5.6, “[HTTP message signing](https://openid.bitbucket.io/fapi/fapi-2_0-message-signing.html#section-5.6)” of the “[FAPI 2.0 Message Signing](https://openid.bitbucket.io/fapi/fapi-2_0-message-signing.html)” specification, require all HTTP message signatures to meet the FAPI 2.0 requirements? Or is it sufficient for an HTTP message to include at least one HTTP message signature that satisfies the FAPI 2.0 requirements?

Requiring all HTTP message signatures to comply with the FAPI 2.0 requirements could make it difficult for application-specific HTTP message signatures to coexist with the FAPI 2.0 Message Signing specification. Therefore, my sense is that the specification should not mandate that all HTTP message signatures meet these requirements, and the specification should explicitly state that a single HTTP message signature meeting the requirements is sufficient.
